nodes.name: Discrete analytic function
nodes.statement: A function $f:\mathbb{Z}^2\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}$ is said to be {\em discrete analytic} if \[ \forall (x,y)\in \mathbb{Z}^2,\qquad \dfrac{f(x+1,y+1)-f(x,y)}{1+i}=\dfrac{f(x+1,y)-f(x,y+1)}{1-i}.\]
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
nodes.statement_short: Discrete analyticity on $\mathbb{Z}^2$: discrete Cauchy-Riemann equation on each lattice square.
nodes.label: maindef

nodes.name: Discrete Cauchy-Riemann equation
nodes.statement: \forall (x,y)\in \mathbb{Z}^2,\qquad \dfrac{f(x+1,y+1)-f(x,y)}{1+i}=\dfrac{f(x+1,y)-f(x,y+1)}{1-i}.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction

nodes.name: Pointwise powers of z: z and z^2 discrete analytic, z^3 not
nodes.statement: For example, the functions $z:=x+iy$ and $z^2$ are discrete analytic in the sense of Definition \ref{maindef}, but $z^3$ is not.

nodes.name: Isaacs' conjecture on monodiffric rational functions
nodes.statement: In \cite{MR0052526} R. Isaacs has posed a conjecture that {\em all monodiffric rational functions are polynomials.}
nodes.section: 1 Introduction
conclusions: all monodiffric rational functions are polynomials.

nodes.name: Harman's counterexample to Isaacs' conjecture
nodes.statement: This conjecture was disproved by C. Harman in \cite{MR0361111}, where an explicit example of a non-polynomial monodiffric function, rational in one quadrant, was constructed.
nodes.section: 1 Introduction

nodes.name: Falling factorial polynomial x^{[n]}
nodes.statement: In what follows, $\Omega$ stands for one of two sets: $\mathbb{Z}$ or $\mathbb{Z}_+$, and $x^{[n]}$ denotes the polynomial of degree $n$ defined by \[ x^{[n]}:=\prod_{j=0}^{n-1}(x-j)\] (if $n=0,$ $x^{[0]}:=1$).

nodes.statement: They have the generating function \[ (1+t)^x=\sum_{k=0}^x x^{[k]}\frac{t^k}{k!}, \] and their discrete analytic extensions $\zeta_n(x,y)$ are studied in section \ref{sec5}.

nodes.name: Difference operator delta
nodes.statement: The linear {\em difference operator} $\delta$ on the space of functions $f:\Omega\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}$ is defined by $$(\delta f)(x)=f(x+1)-f(x),\quad x\in\Omega.$$

nodes.name: Finiteness of the series check f
nodes.statement: Let $f:\mathbb{Z}_+\longrightarrow \mathbb{C}$. Then, for every $x\in\mathbb{Z}_+$ the series $$\check f(x):=\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}_+}f(n)x^{[n]}$$ has a finite number of non zero terms.
nodes.section: 2 Polynomials and rational functions on the set of integers
conclusions: for every $x\in\mathbb{Z}_+$ the series $$\check f(x):=\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}_+}f(n)x^{[n]}$$ has a finite number of non zero terms.
nodes.label: tay1

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 2.2
nodes.statement: In view of \eqref{poly}, $$\forall x\in\mathbb{Z}_+,\,\,\forall n\in\mathbb{Z}_+,\qquad x<n\Longrightarrow x^{[n]}=0.$$ Therefore, for every $x\in\mathbb{Z}_+$ the series $\check f(x)$ contains at most $x+1$ non-zero terms.
nodes.section: 2 Polynomials and rational functions on the set of integers
nodes.statement_short: Direct: $x^{[n]}=0$ for $n>x$, so at most $x+1$ terms survive.

nodes.name: Newton series expansion on Z_+
nodes.statement: Let $f:\mathbb{Z}_+\longrightarrow \mathbb{C}$. Then there exists a unique function $\hat f:\mathbb{Z}_+\longrightarrow \mathbb{C}$ such that \[\forall x\in\mathbb{Z}_+,\qquad f(x)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}_+} \hat f(n)x^{[n]}.\] The function $\hat f(n)$ is given by \[\hat f(n)=\dfrac{(\delta^nf)(0)}{n!}.\]
nodes.section: 2 Polynomials and rational functions on the set of integers
nodes.statement_short: Every $f$ on $\mathbb{Z}_+$ has a unique Newton series in $x^{[n]}$ with coefficients $(\delta^nf)(0)/n!$.
nodes.label: tay2

nodes.name: Newton series of f
nodes.statement: \forall x\in\mathbb{Z}_+,\qquad f(x)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}_+} \hat f(n)x^{[n]}.
nodes.section: 2 Polynomials and rational functions on the set of integers

nodes.name: Fourier coefficients via differences
nodes.statement: \hat f(n)=\dfrac{(\delta^nf)(0)}{n!}.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 2.3
nodes.statement: To show the uniqueness of $\hat f(n)$, assume that \eqref{tay} holds for some function $\hat f(n)$ and apply the identity \[\delta x^{[n]}=nx^{[n-1]}\] repeatedly to obtain \eqref{fou1}.\\ Next, let the function $\hat f(n)$ be defined by \eqref{fou1}. Then, according to Proposition \ref{tay1}, the series $$\tilde f(x):=\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}_+} \hat f(n)x^{[n]}$$ converges absolutely for every $x\in\mathbb{Z}_+$ and defines a function $\tilde f:\mathbb{Z}_+\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}.$ Hence \eqref{fou1} holds with $\tilde f$ replacing $f$ and $$\forall n\in\mathbb{Z}_+,\qquad (\delta^nf)(0)=n! \hat f(n)=(\delta^n\tilde f)(0).$$ Now one can verify that \[\forall x\in\mathbb{Z}_+,\,\,\forall n\in\mathbb{Z}_+,\qquad (\delta^nf)(x)=(\delta^n\tilde f)(x) \] by induction on $x$: If $$ \forall n\in\mathbb{Z}_+, \qquad (\delta^nf)(x)=(\delta^n\tilde f)(x)$$ then \begin{multline*} \forall n\in\mathbb{Z}_+, \qquad (\delta^nf)(x+1)=(\delta^nf)(x)+(\delta^{n+1}f)(x)\\= (\delta^n\tilde f)(x)+(\delta^{n+1}\tilde f)(x) =(\delta^n\tilde f)(x+1).\end{multline*} It remains to set $n=0$ in \eqref{hu1} to obtain \eqref{tay}.
nodes.section: 2 Polynomials and rational functions on the set of integers
nodes.statement_short: Uniqueness by applying $\delta x^{[n]}=nx^{[n-1]}$ repeatedly; existence by building the series and checking all differences agree by induction on $x$.

nodes.statement: \delta x^{[n]}=nx^{[n-1]}

nodes.name: Equality of all differences

nodes.statement: Let $f:\mathbb{Z}_+\longrightarrow \mathbb{C}$. Then the function $\hat f:\mathbb{Z}_+\longrightarrow\mathbb{C},$ defined by \eqref{fou1}, is said to be the Fourier transform of $f$.

nodes.name: Polynomial function on Z
nodes.statement: Suppose that a function $f:\mathbb{Z}\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}$ is such that $$\forall x\in\mathbb{Z},\qquad f(x)=p(x),$$ where $p(x)$ is a polynomial with complex coefficients. Then such a polynomial $p(x)$ is unique, and we shall call the function $f$ itself a polynomial.

nodes.name: Degree of a polynomial function on Z
nodes.statement: If $f(x)\not\equiv 0,$ the degree of $f(x)$ is the same as the degree of $p(x)$.

nodes.name: Finite Newton expansion of polynomials on Z
nodes.statement: Let $f:\mathbb{Z}\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}$ be a polynomial, and let $\hat f :\mathbb{Z}_+\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}$ be the Fourier transform of the restriction $f_{|_{\mathbb{Z}_+}}$. Then the function $\hat f$ has a finite support and $$\forall x\in\mathbb{Z},\qquad f(x)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}_+}\hat f(n)x^{[n]}.$$
nodes.section: 2 Polynomials and rational functions on the set of integers
assumptions: Let $f:\mathbb{Z}\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}$ be a polynomial, and let $\hat f :\mathbb{Z}_+\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}$ be the Fourier transform of the restriction $f_{|_{\mathbb{Z}_+}}$.
conclusions: the function $\hat f$ has a finite support and $$\forall x\in\mathbb{Z},\qquad f(x)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}_+}\hat f(n)x^{[n]}.$$
nodes.label: p01

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 2.5
nodes.statement: Note that $$\deg(\delta f)=\deg(f)-1$$ (if $f=\mathrm{const},$ $\delta f=0$). Hence $$\forall n\in\mathbb{Z}_+,\qquad n>\deg(f)\Longrightarrow \delta^nf=0.$$ Since $$(\delta f)_{|_{\mathbb{Z}_+}}=\delta(f_{|_{\mathbb{Z}_+}}),$$ \eqref{fou1} implies that $$\forall n>\deg(f),\qquad \hat f(n)=0.$$ It follows that $$\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}_+}\hat f(n)x^{[n]}$$ is, in fact, a polynomial, which coincides with the polynomial $f(x)$ on $\mathbb{Z}_+$ and hence on $\mathbb{Z}$.
nodes.section: 2 Polynomials and rational functions on the set of integers
nodes.statement_short: Differencing lowers degree, so high Fourier coefficients vanish and the finite series agrees with $f$.

nodes.name: Difference of a polynomial on Z is a polynomial
nodes.statement: It follows from Proposition \ref{p01} and identity \eqref{hu2} that if $f:\mathbb{Z}\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}$ is a polynomial then so is $\delta f$.
nodes.section: 2 Polynomials and rational functions on the set of integers

nodes.name: Polynomial antidifference on Z
nodes.statement: Let $f:\mathbb{Z}\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}$ be a polynomial. Then there exists a polynomial $g:\mathbb{Z}\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}$ such that $f(x)\equiv (\delta g)(x).$ If $f(x)\not\equiv0$ then $\deg(g)=\deg(f)+1.$
nodes.section: 2 Polynomials and rational functions on the set of integers
conclusions: there exists a polynomial $g:\mathbb{Z}\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}$ such that $f(x)\equiv (\delta g)(x).$
If $f(x)\not\equiv0$ then $\deg(g)=\deg(f)+1.$
nodes.label: p03

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 2.6
nodes.statement: By Proposition \ref{p01}, $$ f(x)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}_+}\hat f(n)x^{[n]},$$ where $\hat f:\mathbb{Z}_+\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}$ is a function with finite support. Consider the polynomial $$g(x)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}_+}\dfrac{\hat{f}(n)}{n+1}x^{[n+1]},$$ then, in view of \eqref{hu2}, $$\forall x\in\mathbb{Z},\qquad (\delta g)(x)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}_+}{\hat{f}(n)}x^{[n]}=f(x).$$
nodes.section: 2 Polynomials and rational functions on the set of integers
nodes.statement_short: Construct $g$ by shifting the Newton series indices and dividing by $n+1$.

nodes.name: Rational function on Z_+
nodes.statement: A function $f:\mathbb{Z}_+\longrightarrow \mathbb{C}$ is said to be {\em rational} if there exist polynomials $p,q:\mathbb{Z}_+\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}$ such that $$\forall x\in \mathbb{Z}_+,\qquad q(x)\not=0,$$ and $$\forall x\in \mathbb{Z}_+,\qquad f(x)=\dfrac{p(x)}{q(x)}.$$
nodes.section: 2 Polynomials and rational functions on the set of integers
nodes.label: defrat1

nodes.name: Realization of rational functions on Z_+
nodes.statement: Let $f:\mathbb{Z}_+\longrightarrow \mathbb{C}$ be given. Then $f(x)$ is a rational function if and only if there exist a polynomial $p(x)$ and matrices $A,B,C$ such that \[ \sigma(A)\cap\mathbb{Z}_+=\emptyset, \] and \begin{equation} f(x)=p(x)+C(xI-A)^{-1}B. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 2 Polynomials and rational functions on the set of integers
nodes.statement_short: $f$ is rational iff $f(x)=p(x)+C(xI-A)^{-1}B$ with $\sigma(A)$ avoiding $\mathbb{Z}_+$.
nodes.label: ABC

nodes.name: Spectrum condition on A
nodes.statement: \sigma(A)\cap\mathbb{Z}_+=\emptyset,
nodes.section: 2 Polynomials and rational functions on the set of integers

nodes.name: Realization formula for f
nodes.section: 2 Polynomials and rational functions on the set of integers
nodes.label: eqreal

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 2.8
nodes.statement: We first recall that a matrix-valued rational function of a complex variable can always be written in the form \[ r(z)=p(z)+C(zI-A)^{-1}B, \] where the matrix-valued polynomial $p$ takes care of the pole at infinity, and $A,B$ and $C$ are matrices of appropriate sizes. Furthermore, when the dimension of $A$ is minimal, the (finite) poles of $r$ coincide with the spectrum of $A$; see \cite{bgk1, MR0255260}. Here, we consider complex-valued functions, and thus $C$ and $B$ are respectively a row and column vector.\\ Now, by Definition \ref{defrat1}, $f$ is a rational function if and only if it is the restriction on $\mathbb{Z}_+$ of a rational function of a complex variable, with no poles on $\mathbb{Z}_+$, that is if and only if it can be written as \eqref{eqreal} with the matrix $A$ satisfying furthermore \eqref{kaas}.
nodes.section: 2 Polynomials and rational functions on the set of integers
nodes.statement_short: Recall the state-space realization of rational matrix functions and restrict to $\mathbb{Z}_+$.

nodes.name: Realization of matrix-valued rational functions
nodes.statement: We first recall that a matrix-valued rational function of a complex variable can always be written in the form \[ r(z)=p(z)+C(zI-A)^{-1}B, \] where the matrix-valued polynomial $p$ takes care of the pole at infinity, and $A,B$ and $C$ are matrices of appropriate sizes. Furthermore, when the dimension of $A$ is minimal, the (finite) poles of $r$ coincide with the spectrum of $A$; see \cite{bgk1, MR0255260}.
nodes.section: 2 Polynomials and rational functions on the set of integers
nodes.origin_citation: Bart, Gohberg, Kaashoek 1979; Kalman, Falb, Arbib 1969
nodes.statement_short: A matrix rational function is $p(z)+C(zI-A)^{-1}B$; for minimal $A$ the finite poles are $\sigma(A)$.

nodes.name: Growth bound on Fourier coefficients of rational functions
nodes.statement: Let $f:\mathbb{Z}_+\longrightarrow \mathbb{C}$ be rational, and let $\hat {f}:\mathbb{Z}_+\longrightarrow \mathbb{C}$ be the Fourier transform of $f$. Then $$\limsup_{n\rightarrow\infty}(|\hat f(n)|n!)^{1/n}\leq 1.$$
nodes.section: 2 Polynomials and rational functions on the set of integers
assumptions: Let $f:\mathbb{Z}_+\longrightarrow \mathbb{C}$ be rational, and let $\hat {f}:\mathbb{Z}_+\longrightarrow \mathbb{C}$ be the Fourier transform of $f$.
conclusions: $$\limsup_{n\rightarrow\infty}(|\hat f(n)|n!)^{1/n}\leq 1.$$
nodes.label: lim1

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 2.9
nodes.statement: According to Proposition \ref{ABC}, there exist a polynomial $p(x)$ and matrices $A,B,C$ such that $\sigma(A)\cap\mathbb{Z}_+=\emptyset$ and $$f(x)=p(x)+C(xI-A)^{-1}B.$$ Hence, for $n>\deg(p)$, $$|\hat{f}(n)n!|=|(\delta^nf)(0)|\leq\|C\|\cdot\|B\|\cdot\|A^{-1}\|\cdot \prod_{j=1}^n\|\left(I-\dfrac{1}{n}A\right)^{-1}\|.$$ Since $$\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\|\left(I-\dfrac{1}{n}A\right)^{-1}\|=1,$$ $$\forall\epsilon>0,\,\,\exists M,N\in\mathbb{Z}_+,\,\forall n\in\mathbb{Z}_+\quad:\quad n\geq N\Longrightarrow|\hat{f}(n)n!|\leq M(1+\epsilon)^n,$$ and the conclusion follows.
nodes.section: 2 Polynomials and rational functions on the set of integers
nodes.statement_short: Use the realization of Proposition 2.8 to bound $(\delta^nf)(0)$ by a product of resolvent norms tending to 1.

nodes.name: Partial difference operators delta_x, delta_y
nodes.statement: The linear {\em difference operators} $\delta_x,\delta_y$ on the space of functions $f:\Omega_1\times\Omega_2\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}$ are defined by $$(\delta_xf)(x,y):=f(x+1,y)-f(x,y),\quad (\delta_yf)(x,y):=f(x,y+1)-f(x,y).$$
nodes.section: 3 Discrete polynomials of two variables

nodes.name: Commutation of delta_x and delta_y
nodes.statement: Note that the difference operators $\delta_x$ and $\delta_y$ commute: \[ (\delta_x\delta_yf)(x,y)= (\delta_y\delta_xf)(x,y)=f(x+1,y+1)-f(x,y+1)-f(x+1,y)+f(x,y). \]
nodes.section: 3 Discrete polynomials of two variables

nodes.name: Commutation identity
nodes.statement: (\delta_x\delta_yf)(x,y)= (\delta_y\delta_xf)(x,y)=f(x+1,y+1)-f(x,y+1)-f(x+1,y)+f(x,y).
nodes.section: 3 Discrete polynomials of two variables

nodes.name: Finiteness of the two-variable series
nodes.statement: Let $f:\mathbb{Z}_+^2\longrightarrow \mathbb{C}$. Then for every $(x,y)\in\mathbb{Z}_+^2$, the series \[ \check f(x,y):=\sum_{(m,n)\in\mathbb{Z}_+^2}f(m,n)x^{[m]}y^{[n]} \] contains finitely many non-zero terms.
nodes.section: 3 Discrete polynomials of two variables
nodes.label: tay11

nodes.name: Two-variable transform
nodes.statement: \check f(x,y):=\sum_{(m,n)\in\mathbb{Z}_+^2}f(m,n)x^{[m]}y^{[n]}
nodes.section: 3 Discrete polynomials of two variables

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3.2
nodes.statement: In view of \eqref{poly}, $$\forall x\in\mathbb{Z}_+,\,\forall n\in\mathbb{Z}_+,\,\quad x<n\Longrightarrow x^{[n]}=0.$$ Therefore, for every $(x,y)\in\mathbb{Z}_+^2$ the series $\check f(x)$ contains at most $(x+1)(y+1)$ non-zero terms.
nodes.section: 3 Discrete polynomials of two variables
nodes.statement_short: Direct: $x^{[m]}y^{[n]}$ vanishes unless $m\le x$, $n\le y$.

nodes.name: Two-variable Newton series expansion
nodes.statement: Let $f:\mathbb{Z}_+^2\longrightarrow \mathbb{C}$. Then there exists a unique function $\hat f:\mathbb{Z}_+^2\longrightarrow \mathbb{C}$ such that \[\forall (x,y)\in\mathbb{Z}_+^2, \qquad f(x,y)=\sum_{(m,n)\in\mathbb{Z}_+^2} \hat f(m,n)x^{[m]}y^{[n]}. \] The function $\hat f(m,n)$ is given by \[ \hat f(m,n)=\dfrac{(\delta_x^m\delta_y^nf)(0,0)}{m!n!}, \quad (m,n)\in\mathbb{Z}_+^2.\]
nodes.section: 3 Discrete polynomials of two variables
nodes.statement_short: Every $f$ on $\mathbb{Z}_+^2$ has a unique double Newton series with coefficients $(\delta_x^m\delta_y^nf)(0,0)/(m!n!)$.
nodes.label: tay12

nodes.name: Double Newton series
nodes.statement: \forall (x,y)\in\mathbb{Z}_+^2, \qquad f(x,y)=\sum_{(m,n)\in\mathbb{Z}_+^2} \hat f(m,n)x^{[m]}y^{[n]}.
nodes.section: 3 Discrete polynomials of two variables

nodes.name: Two-variable Fourier coefficients
nodes.statement: \hat f(m,n)=\dfrac{(\delta_x^m\delta_y^nf)(0,0)}{m!n!}, \quad (m,n)\in\mathbb{Z}_+^2.
nodes.section: 3 Discrete polynomials of two variables

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3.3
nodes.statement: First, fix $x\in\mathbb{Z}_+$ and consider the function $f_x:\mathbb{Z}_+\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}$ given by $$f_x(y)=f(x,y),\quad y\in\mathbb{Z}_+.$$ Then, according to Proposition \ref{tay2}, there is a unique function $\hat{ f_x}:\mathbb{Z}_+\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}$ such that $$\forall y\in\mathbb{Z}_+,\qquad f_x(y)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}_+}\hat{f_x}(n) y^{[n]};$$ the function $\hat{f_x}(n)$ is given by $$\hat{f_x}(n)=\dfrac{(\delta_y^n f)(x,0)}{n!},\quad n\in\mathbb{Z}_+.$$ Next, fix $n\in\mathbb{Z}_+$ and consider the function $g_n:\mathbb{Z}_+\longrightarrow \mathbb{C}$ given by $$g_n(x)=\hat{f_x}(n),\quad x\in\mathbb{Z}_+.$$ By the same Proposition \ref{tay2}, there is a unique function $\hat{g_n}:\mathbb{Z}_+\longrightarrow \mathbb{C}$ such that $$\forall x\in\mathbb{Z}_+,\qquad g_n(x)=\sum_{m\in\mathbb{Z}_+}\hat{g_n}(m) x^{[m]};$$ the function $\hat{g_n}(m)$ is given by $$\hat{g_n}(m)=\dfrac{(\delta_x^m\delta_y^n f)(0,0)}{m!n!},\quad m\in\mathbb{Z}_+.$$ Thus $$\forall (x,y)\in\mathbb{Z}_+^2,\qquad f(x,y)=\sum_{(m,n) \in\mathbb{Z}_+^2}\hat{g_n}(m) x^{[m]}y^{[n]}.$$ It remains to set $\hat f(m,n)=\hat{g_n}(m).$
nodes.section: 3 Discrete polynomials of two variables
nodes.statement_short: Apply the one-variable expansion (Proposition 2.3) first in $y$ for fixed $x$, then in $x$ for each coefficient.

nodes.name: Fourier transform on Z_+^2
nodes.statement: Let $f:\mathbb{Z}_+^2\longrightarrow \mathbb{C}$. Then the function $\hat f:\mathbb{Z}_+^2\longrightarrow\mathbb{C},$ defined by \eqref{fou11}, is said to be the Fourier transform of $f$.

nodes.name: Polynomials vanishing on Z^2 vanish identically
nodes.statement: Let $p(z,w)$ be a complex polynomial in two variables. Then, $p\big|_{\mathbb{Z}^2}=0$ if and only if $p\equiv 0$.
nodes.section: 3 Discrete polynomials of two variables
assumptions: Let $p(z,w)$ be a complex polynomial in two variables.
conclusions: $p\big|_{\mathbb{Z}^2}=0$ if and only if $p\equiv 0$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3.5
nodes.statement: Write \[ p(z,w)=\sum_{n=0}^N p_n(z)w^n, \] where the $p_n$ are polynomials in $z$. The equations $p(z,w)\equiv 0$ for $w=0,1,\ldots N$ lead to (using a Vandermonde determinant) that $p_0(z),p_1(z),\ldots, p_N(z)$ vanish on $\mathbb{Z}$ and hence identically.
nodes.section: 3 Discrete polynomials of two variables
nodes.statement_short: Expand in powers of $w$ and use a Vandermonde determinant to show each coefficient polynomial vanishes on $\mathbb{Z}$.

nodes.statement: Suppose that a function $f:\mathbb{Z}^2\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}$ is such that $$\forall (x,y)\in\mathbb{Z}^2,\qquad f(x,y)=p(x,y),$$ where $p(x,y)$ is a polynomial with complex coefficients. Then in view of Theorem \ref{tautology}, such a polynomial $p(x,y)$ is unique, and we shall call the function $f$ itself a polynomial.

Then the function $\hat f$ has a finite support and $$\forall (x,y)\in\mathbb{Z}^2,\quad f(x,y)=\sum_{(m,n)\in\mathbb{Z}_+^2}\hat f(m,n)x^{[m]}y^{[n]}.$$

assumptions: Let $f:\mathbb{Z}^2\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}$ be a polynomial, and let $\hat f :\mathbb{Z}_+^2\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}$ be the Fourier transform of the restriction $f_{|_{\mathbb{Z}_+^2}}$.
conclusions: the function $\hat f$ has a finite support and $$\forall (x,y)\in\mathbb{Z}^2,\quad f(x,y)=\sum_{(m,n)\in\mathbb{Z}_+^2}\hat f(m,n)x^{[m]}y^{[n]}.$$

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3.6
nodes.statement: First, in view of \eqref{fou11} and of the fact that $$\forall (m,n)\in\mathbb{Z}_+^2,\,\,\forall (x,y)\in\mathbb{Z}^2, \quad m+n>\deg(f)\Longrightarrow (\delta_x^m\delta_y^n f)(x,y)=0,$$ the function $\hat f$ has a finite support. It follows that $$\sum_{(m,n)\in\mathbb{Z}_+^2}\hat f(m,n)x^{[m]}y^{[n]}$$ is, in fact, a polynomial, which coincides with the polynomial $f(x,y)$ on $\mathbb{Z}_+^2$ and hence on $\mathbb{Z}^2$.
nodes.section: 3 Discrete polynomials of two variables
nodes.statement_short: High-order differences of a polynomial vanish, so the transform has finite support and the series is a polynomial agreeing with $f$.

nodes.name: Partial differences of a polynomial on Z^2 are polynomials
nodes.statement: It follows from Proposition \ref{p11} and identity \eqref{hu2} that if $f:\mathbb{Z}^2\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}$ is a polynomial then so are $\delta_x f$ and $\delta_yf$.

nodes.name: Discrete exactness: compatible polynomials have a common antidifference
nodes.statement: Let $f,g:\mathbb{Z}^2\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}$ be two polynomials, such that \[(\delta_y f)(x,y)\equiv(\delta_x g)(x,y).\] Then there exists a polynomial $h:\mathbb{Z}^2\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}$ such that \[(\delta_xh)(x,y)\equiv f(x,y),\quad (\delta_yh)(x,y)\equiv g(x,y).\]
nodes.section: 3 Discrete polynomials of two variables
assumptions: Let $f,g:\mathbb{Z}^2\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}$ be two polynomials, such that \[ (\delta_y f)(x,y)\equiv(\delta_x g)(x,y).\]
nodes.statement_short: If $\delta_yf=\delta_xg$ for polynomials $f,g$, there is a polynomial $h$ with $\delta_xh=f$, $\delta_yh=g$.

nodes.statement: (\delta_y f)(x,y)\equiv(\delta_x g)(x,y).

nodes.statement: (\delta_xh)(x,y)\equiv f(x,y),\quad (\delta_yh)(x,y)\equiv g(x,y).

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3.7
nodes.statement: By Proposition \ref{p11}, there exist functions $\hat f,\hat g:\mathbb{Z}_+^2\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}$ with finite support, such that $$f(x,y)=\sum_{(m,n)\in\mathbb{Z}_+^2}\hat{f}(m,n)x^{[m]}y^{[n]},\quad g(x,y)=\sum_{(m,n)\in\mathbb{Z}_+^2}\hat{g}(m,n)x^{[m]}y^{[n]}.$$ Then identity \eqref{co01} implies that \[\forall (m,n)\in\mathbb{Z}^2_+,\qquad (n+1)\hat{f}(m,n+1)=(m+1)\hat{g}(m+1,n).\] Consider the polynomial $$h(x,y)=\sum_{(m,n)\in\mathbb{Z}_+^2}\dfrac{\hat{f}(m,n)}{m+1} x^{[m+1]}y^{[n]}+\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}_+}\dfrac{\hat{g}(0,n)}{n+1}y^{[n+1]},$$ then $$\forall (x,y)\in\mathbb{Z}^2,\qquad(\delta_x h)(x,y)=\sum_{(m,n)\in\mathbb{Z}_+^2}\hat{f}(m,n) x^{[m]}y^{[n]}=f(x,y).$$ On the other hand, in view of \eqref{use03}, $$h(x,y)=\sum_{(m,n)\in\mathbb{Z}_+^2}\dfrac{\hat{g}(m,n)}{n+1} x^{[m]}y^{[n+1]}+\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}_+}\dfrac{\hat{f}(m,0)}{m+1}x^{[m+1]},$$ hence $$\forall (x,y)\in\mathbb{Z}^2,\qquad(\delta_y h)(x,y)=\sum_{(m,n)\in\mathbb{Z}_+^2}\hat{g}(m,n) x^{[m]}y^{[n]}=g(x,y).$$
nodes.section: 3 Discrete polynomials of two variables
nodes.statement_short: Expand $f,g$ in double Newton series, derive a coefficient relation, and construct $h$ explicitly.

nodes.name: Coefficient relation
nodes.statement: \forall (m,n)\in\mathbb{Z}^2_+,\qquad (n+1)\hat{f}(m,n+1)=(m+1)\hat{g}(m+1,n).

nodes.name: Discrete Cauchy-Riemann operator characterization
nodes.statement: A function $f:\Omega_1\times\Omega_2\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}$ is discrete analytic if and only if $$\forall (x,y)\in \Omega_1\times\Omega_2,\qquad(\bar\mathcal{D} f)(x,y)=0,$$ where \[\bar\mathcal{D}:=(1-i)\delta_x+(1+i)\delta_y+\delta_x\delta_y.\]
nodes.section: 4 Discrete analytic polynomials
nodes.statement_short: $f$ is discrete analytic iff $\bar{\mathcal D}f=0$, with $\bar{\mathcal D}=(1-i)\delta_x+(1+i)\delta_y+\delta_x\delta_y$.
nodes.label: maindef2

nodes.name: Discrete del-bar operator
nodes.statement: \bar\mathcal{D}:=(1-i)\delta_x+(1+i)\delta_y+\delta_x\delta_y.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4.1
nodes.statement: In view of \eqref{comm}, \begin{multline*}\forall(x,y)\in\Omega_1\times\Omega_2,\quad \dfrac{f(x+1,y+1)-f(x,y)}{1+i}-\dfrac{f(x+1,y)-f(x,y+1)}{1-i}\\= \dfrac{1-i}{2}(f(x+1,y+1)-f(x,y)-if(x+1,y)+if(x,y+1))\\= \dfrac{1-i}{2}((\delta_x\delta_yf)(x,y)-2f(x,y)+ (1-i)f(x+1,y)+(1+i)f(x,y+1))\\=\dfrac{1-i}{2}((\delta_x\delta_yf)(x,y)+ (1-i)(\delta_xf)(x,y)+(1+i)(\delta_yf)(x,y)).\end{multline*}
nodes.section: 4 Discrete analytic polynomials
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite the discrete Cauchy-Riemann difference in terms of $\delta_x,\delta_y$ using commutation.

nodes.name: Unique discrete analytic polynomial extension (Duffin)
nodes.statement: Let $p:\mathbb{Z}\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}$ be a polynomial. Then there exists a unique discrete analytic polynomial $q:\mathbb{Z}^2\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}$ such that $$\forall x\in\mathbb{Z},\qquad q(x,0)= p(x).$$ In particular, $q(x,y)\equiv 0$ if and only if $p(x)\equiv 0$. If this is not the case, $$\deg(q)=\deg(p).$$
nodes.section: 4 Discrete analytic polynomials
conclusions: there exists a unique discrete analytic polynomial $q:\mathbb{Z}^2\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}$ such that $$\forall x\in\mathbb{Z},\qquad q(x,0)= p(x).$$
In particular, $q(x,y)\equiv 0$ if and only if $p(x)\equiv 0$.
If this is not the case, $$\deg(q)=\deg(p).$$
nodes.label: t1

nodes.name: Vanishing on the axis forces vanishing
nodes.statement: Let $q:\mathbb{Z}^2\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}$ be a discrete analytic polynomial, such that $q(x,0)\equiv 0.$ Then $q(x,y)\equiv 0.$
nodes.section: 4 Discrete analytic polynomials
assumptions: Let $q:\mathbb{Z}^2\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}$ be a discrete analytic polynomial, such that $q(x,0)\equiv 0.$
conclusions: $q(x,y)\equiv 0.$
nodes.label: l1

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 4.3
nodes.statement: Assume the opposite, then $\deg(q)>0,$ and $q$ can be chosen so that $\deg q$ is the smallest possible. Observe that $(\delta_xq)(x,y)$ is also a discrete analytic polynomial, that $ (\delta_xq)(x,0)\equiv 0,$ and that $\deg(\delta_xp)<\deg(p).$ Hence $(\delta_xq)(x,y)\equiv 0.$ Since $q(x,y)$ is discrete analytic, Definition \ref{maindef2} implies that $$\forall (x,y)\in\mathbb{Z}^2,\qquad (\delta_yq)(x,y)= \dfrac{i-1}{2}((1-i+\delta_y)\delta_xq)(x,y)= 0.$$ Thus $$(\delta_xq)(x,y)\equiv(\delta_yq)(x,y)\equiv 0$$ and hence $q=\mathrm{const}$ - a contradiction.
nodes.section: 4 Discrete analytic polynomials
nodes.statement_short: Minimal-degree counterexample: $\delta_xq$ has lower degree so vanishes, then $\delta_yq=0$ by the Cauchy-Riemann operator, so $q$ is constant.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 4.2
nodes.statement: The uniqueness of the polynomial $q(x,y)$ follows from Lemma \ref{l1}. The existence in the case $p=\mathrm{const}$ is clear: it suffices to set $$q(x,y)=p(0).$$ If $p\not=\mathrm{const}$ we proceed by induction on $d=\deg(p)$. According to Proposition \ref{p03}, $(\delta p)(x)$ is a polynomial and $\deg(\delta p)=d-1$. Therefore, by the induction assumption, there is a discrete analytic polynomial $f(x,y)$, such that $$\forall x\in\mathbb{Z},\qquad f(x,0)=(\delta p)(x)$$ and $\deg(f)=d-1.$ Let $g:\mathbb{Z}^2\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}$ be defined by $$g(x,y)=if(x,y)-\dfrac{1-i}{2}(\delta_yf)(x,y),$$ then $g(x,y)$ is also a discrete analytic polynomial, $\deg(g)=d-1.$ Furthermore, since $(\bar Df)(x,y)\equiv 0,$ \begin{multline*}\forall (x,y)\in\mathbb{Z}^2,\quad (\delta_xg)(x,y)=i(\delta_xf)(x,y)-\dfrac{1-i}{2}(\delta_x\delta_yf)(x,y)\\= i(\delta_xf)(x,y)+\dfrac{1-i}{2}((1-i)(\delta_xf)(x,y)+(1+i)(\delta_yf)(x,y))= (\delta_yf)(x,y).\end{multline*} Hence, according to Proposition \ref{p13}, there exists a polynomial $h:\mathbb{Z}^2\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}$ such that $$(\delta_xh)(x,y)\equiv f(x,y),\quad (\delta_y h)(x,y)\equiv g(x,y).$$ Since $$\forall (x,y)\in\mathbb{Z}^2,\qquad (\bar D h)(x,y)=(1-i)f(x,y)+(1+i)g(x,y)+(\delta_y f)(x,y)=0,$$ the polynomial $h(x,y)$ is discrete analytic. Finally, since $$\forall x\in\mathbb{Z},\qquad (\delta_x h)(x,0)=f(x,0)=(\delta p)(x),$$ $h(x,0)-p(x)$ is a constant function. Thus it suffices to set $$q(x,y)=h(x,y)-h(0,0)+p(0)$$ to complete the proof.
nodes.section: 4 Discrete analytic polynomials
nodes.statement_short: Uniqueness from Lemma 4.3; existence by induction on $\deg p$. The inductive step builds $h$ with $\delta_xh=f$, $\delta_yh=g$ via Proposition 3.7.

nodes.name: Discrete analytic polynomials zeta_n
nodes.statement: In view of Theorem \ref{t1}, there exists a unique discrete analytic polynomial $\zeta_n(x,y)$ determined by $$\zeta_n(x,0)\equiv x^{[n]}.$$

nodes.name: Argument for the identity delta_x zeta_n = n zeta_{n-1}
nodes.statement: Then (as follows from Proposition \ref{p11} and identities \eqref{hu2}, \eqref{comm}) $(\delta_x\zeta_n)(x,y)$ is also a discrete analytic polynomial such that $$(\delta_x\zeta_n)(x,0)\equiv \delta x^{[n]}\equiv nx^{[n-1]}.$$
nodes.section: 5 Expandable discrete analytic functions
nodes.statement_short: Differences of $\zeta_n$ are discrete analytic polynomials restricting to $nx^{[n-1]}$.

nodes.name: Lowering identity for zeta_n
nodes.statement: Hence, by the uniqueness part of Theorem \ref{t1}, \[ (\delta_x\zeta_n)(x,y)\equiv n\zeta_{n-1}(x,y)\] (if $n=0$, $\zeta_0(x,y)\equiv 1$ and $(\delta_x\zeta_0)(x,y)\equiv 0$).

conclusions: \[(\delta_x\zeta_n)(x,y)\equiv n\zeta_{n-1}(x,y)\]

nodes.statement: (\delta_x\zeta_n)(x,y)\equiv n\zeta_{n-1}(x,y)

nodes.name: Generating function of the zeta_n
nodes.statement: For each $(x,y)\in\mathbb{Z}^2$ the function \[ e_{x,y}(z)=(1+z)^x\left(\dfrac{1+i+iz}{1+i+z}\right)^y, \] is analytic (in the usual sense) in the variable $z$ in the open unit disk $\mathbb D$, and admits the Taylor expansion \begin{equation} e_{x,y}(z)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}_+}\dfrac{z^n \zeta_n(x,y)}{n!},\quad \forall z\in\mathbb{D}. \end{equation}
nodes.section: 5 Expandable discrete analytic functions
nodes.statement_short: $e_{x,y}(z)=(1+z)^x((1+i+iz)/(1+i+z))^y$ is analytic in the disk with Taylor coefficients $\zeta_n(x,y)/n!$.
nodes.label: prop6.1

nodes.name: Generating function e_{x,y}(z)
nodes.statement: e_{x,y}(z)=(1+z)^x\left(\dfrac{1+i+iz}{1+i+z}\right)^y,

nodes.name: Taylor expansion of e_{x,y}
nodes.statement: e_{x,y}(z)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}_+}\dfrac{z^n \zeta_n(x,y)}{n!},\quad \forall z\in\mathbb{D}.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 5.1
nodes.statement: The analyticity is clear because $x,y\in\mathbb{Z}$ and we have $$e_{x,y}(z)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}_+}\dfrac{z^n c_n(x,y)}{n!},\quad \forall z\in\mathbb{D}.$$ where $$c_n(x,y)=\dfrac{d^n}{dz^n}e_{x,y}\Bigm|_{z=0}.$$ Since $$e_{x+1,y}(z)-e_{x,y}(z)=ze_{x,y}(z)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}_+}\dfrac{z^{n+1} c_{n}(x,y)}{n!},$$ $$\forall (x,y)\in\mathbb{Z}^2,\,\,\forall n\in\mathbb{Z}_+,\qquad (\delta_xc_{n})(x,y)=nc_{n-1}(x,y)$$ (if $n=0,$ $c_0(x,y)\equiv 1$ and $(\delta_xc_0)(x,y)\equiv 0$). Similarly, since \[ \begin{split} \dfrac{e_{x+1,y+1}(z)-e_{x,y}(z)}{1+ i}-\dfrac{e_{x+1,y}(z)-e_{x,y+1}(z)}{1-i}&=\\ &\hspace{-5cm}=\left( (1+z)\dfrac{1+i+iz}{1+i+z}-1\right)\dfrac{e_{x,y}(z)}{1+i}-\left( 1+z-\dfrac{1+i+iz}{1+i+z}\right)\dfrac{e_{x,y}(z)}{1-i}\\ &\hspace{-5cm}=0, \end{split} \] we have $$\forall (x,y)\in\mathbb{Z}^2,\,\,{\rm and}\,\,\forall n\in\mathbb{Z}_+,\qquad (\bar Dc_{n})(x,y)=0.$$ Thus, for every $n\in\mathbb{Z}_+$, the function $c_n:\mathbb{Z}^2\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}$ is discrete analytic. Next, we show by induction that \[ \forall n\in\mathbb{Z}_+,\quad c_n(x,y)\equiv\zeta_n(x,y). \] Indeed, for $n=0$, $$c_0(x,y)\equiv 1\equiv\zeta_0(x,y).$$ Assume that, for some $n\in\mathbb{Z}_+$, $$c_n(x,y)\equiv\zeta_n(x,y),$$ then, in view of \eqref{hu3}, $$(\delta_xc_{n+1}(x,y)\equiv(n+1)c_n(x,y)\equiv (n+1)\zeta_n(x,y)\equiv(\delta_x\zeta_{n+1}(x,y),$$ hence $$(\delta_x(\zeta_{n+1}-c_{n+1}))(x,y)\equiv 0.$$ But the functions $c_{n+1}$ and $\zeta_{n+1}$ are discrete analytic, hence $$(\bar D(\zeta_{n+1}-c_{n+1}))(x,y)\equiv 0$$ and $$(\delta_y(\zeta_{n+1}-c_{n+1}))(x,y)\equiv 0.$$ It follows that $$\zeta_{n+1}-c_{n+1}=\mathrm{const};$$ since $$\zeta_{n+1}(0,0)=0=c_{n+1}(0,0),$$ one concludes that $$c_{n+1}(x,y)\equiv\zeta_{n+1}(x,y),$$ and \eqref{hu4} follows.
nodes.section: 5 Expandable discrete analytic functions
nodes.statement_short: Show Taylor coefficients $c_n$ satisfy the lowering identity and are discrete analytic, then $c_n=\zeta_n$ by induction on $n$.

nodes.statement: \forall n\in\mathbb{Z}_+,\quad c_n(x,y)\equiv\zeta_n(x,y).

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 5.2
nodes.statement: Set $y=0$ in $e_{x,y}(z)$ in \eqref{exy}. By \eqref{hu4} we get \[ (1+z)^x=\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}_+}\frac{z^n}{n!}\zeta_n(x,0). \] \eqref{value:zeta:n} follows by comparing the coefficients of $z^n$ in \eqref{eq:y=0}.

nodes.name: Growth of zeta_n
nodes.statement: It holds that $$\forall(x,y)\in\mathbb{Z}_+\times (\mathbb{Z}\setminus\{0\}),\qquad \limsup_{n\rightarrow\infty} \left(\dfrac{|\zeta_n(x,y)|}{n!}\right)^{1/n}= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}.$$
nodes.section: 5 Expandable discrete analytic functions
conclusions: $$\forall(x,y)\in\mathbb{Z}_+\times (\mathbb{Z}\setminus\{0\}),\qquad \limsup_{n\rightarrow\infty} \left(\dfrac{|\zeta_n(x,y)|}{n!}\right)^{1/n}= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}.$$
nodes.label: lim2

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 5.3
nodes.statement: When $x\ge 0$ the function \eqref{exy} is analytic in the variable $z$ in the disk centered at the origin and of radius $\sqrt{2}$, and has a pole on the boundary of this disk. Hence the radius of convergence of the McLaurin series is precisely $\sqrt{2}$, and $$\limsup_{n\rightarrow\infty} \left(\dfrac{|\zeta_n(x,y)|}{n!}\right)^{1/n}= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{2}}.$$
nodes.section: 5 Expandable discrete analytic functions
nodes.statement_short: The generating function has radius of convergence exactly $\sqrt2$ (pole on the boundary).

nodes.name: Series in zeta_n are discrete analytic
nodes.statement: Let $g:\mathbb{Z}_+\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}$ be such that for every $(x,y)\in\mathbb{Z}_+\times\mathbb{Z}$ the series \[f(x,y)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}_+} g(n)\zeta_n(x,y)\] converges absolutely. Then the function $f:\mathbb{Z}_+\times \mathbb{Z}\longrightarrow \mathbb{C}$, defined by \eqref{tay41}, is discrete analytic, and it holds that $$g(n)\equiv \hat{f_0}(n),$$ where the function $f_0:\mathbb{Z}_+\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}$ is given by \[f_0(x)=f(x,0),\quad x\in\mathbb{Z}_+.\]
nodes.section: 5 Expandable discrete analytic functions
nodes.statement_short: An absolutely convergent series $\sum g(n)\zeta_n$ is discrete analytic, with $g$ the Fourier transform of its axis restriction.
nodes.label: p52

nodes.name: Series in zeta_n
nodes.statement: f(x,y)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}_+} g(n)\zeta_n(x,y)

nodes.statement: f_0(x)=f(x,0),\quad x\in\mathbb{Z}_+.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 5.4
nodes.statement: The discrete analyticity of $f$ follows directly from the discrete analyticity of the polynomials $\zeta_n$. Furthermore, when $y=0$ the formula \eqref{tay41} becomes $$f_0(x)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}_+} g(n)x^{[n]},$$ hence, according to Proposition \ref{tay2}, $g=\hat{f_0}$.

nodes.statement_short: Analyticity termwise; set $y=0$ and apply uniqueness of the Newton expansion.

nodes.name: Expandable function
nodes.statement: A function $f:\mathbb{Z}_+\times \mathbb{Z}\longrightarrow \mathbb{C}$ is said to be {\em expandable} if:\begin{enumerate} \item the Fourier transform $\hat{f_0}$ of the function $f_0:\mathbb{Z}_+\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}$, given by \eqref{rest}, satisfies the estimate \begin{equation} \limsup_{n\rightarrow\infty}(|\hat{f_0}(n)|n!)^{1/n}<\sqrt{2}; \end{equation} \item the function $f$ admits the representation $$ f(x,y)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}_+}\hat{f_0}(n)\zeta_n(x,y),\quad (x,y)\in\mathbb{Z}_+\times\mathbb{Z}.$$ \end{enumerate}
nodes.section: 5 Expandable discrete analytic functions
nodes.statement_short: $f$ is expandable if its axis Fourier transform satisfies the growth bound and $f=\sum\hat{f_0}(n)\zeta_n$.

nodes.name: Growth estimate for expandable functions
nodes.statement: \limsup_{n\rightarrow\infty}(|\hat{f_0}(n)|n!)^{1/n}<\sqrt{2};

nodes.name: Expandable functions contain polynomials and are determined on the axis
nodes.statement: The class of expandable functions contains all discrete analytic polynomials, and elements of this class are determined by their values on the positive horizontal axis.

nodes.name: Unique expandable extension of rational functions
nodes.statement: Suppose that $f_0:\mathbb{Z}_+\longrightarrow \mathbb{C}$ is rational. Then there exists a unique expandable function $f:\mathbb{Z}_+\times \mathbb{Z}\longrightarrow \mathbb{C}$ such that $$f(x,0)\equiv f_0(x).$$

conclusions: there exists a unique expandable function $f:\mathbb{Z}_+\times \mathbb{Z}\longrightarrow \mathbb{C}$ such that $$f(x,0)\equiv f_0(x).$$

nodes.name: Cauchy-Kovalevskaya product of expandable functions
nodes.statement: Consider $f_1$ and $f_2$ two expandable functions, and assume that the Fourier transform of the pointwise product $f_1(x,0)f_2(x,0)$ satisfy \eqref{esti}. Then there exists a unique discrete analytic expandable function $g$ such that \[ g(x,0)=f_1(x,0)f_2(x,0) \] $g$ is called the Cauchy-Kovalesvskaya product of $f_1$ and $f_2$ and is denoted by $f_1\odot f_2$.
nodes.section: 6 The Cauchy-Kovalevskaya product
nodes.statement_short: The C-K product $f_1\odot f_2$ is the unique expandable extension of the pointwise product on the axis.

nodes.name: C-K product of rational functions exists
nodes.statement: Note that the Cauchy-Kovalesvskaya product of two rational functions always exist.

nodes.name: Cauchy-Kovalevskaya (C-K) product
nodes.statement: Let $f:\mathbb{Z}^2\longrightarrow \mathbb{C}$ be a polynomial, such that $$f(x,0)\equiv c_0+c_1x+\dots +c_nx^n,$$ and let $g:\Omega\times\mathbb{Z}\longrightarrow \mathbb{C}$ be given. The Cauchy-Kovalevskaya (C-K) product of $f$ and $g$ is defined by \begin{equation} (g\odot f)(x,y)=(f\odot g)(x,y)=c_0g(x,y)+c_1(\mathcal{Z} g)(x,y)+\dots+c_n(\mathcal{Z}^ng)(x,y). \end{equation}
nodes.section: 6 The Cauchy-Kovalevskaya product
nodes.statement_short: For polynomial $f$ with $f(x,0)=\sum c_kx^k$, $f\odot g=\sum c_k\mathcal{Z}^kg$.
nodes.label: formal

nodes.name: C-K product formula
nodes.statement: (g\odot f)(x,y)=(f\odot g)(x,y)=c_0g(x,y)+c_1(\mathcal{Z} g)(x,y)+\dots+c_n(\mathcal{Z}^ng)(x,y).
nodes.section: 6 The Cauchy-Kovalevskaya product
nodes.label: ckdef

nodes.name: Properties of the C-K product
nodes.statement: \mbox{}\\ $(1)$ The restriction of the C-K product to $\mathbb Z_+$ is the product of the restriction.\\ $(2)$ The C-K product is the unique discrete analytic extension corresponding to the product of the restrictions.\\ $(3)$ The C-K product is commutative, i.e. \[ g\odot f=f\odot g \] for all choices of discrete analytic polynomials
nodes.section: 6 The Cauchy-Kovalevskaya product
nodes.statement_short: The C-K product restricts to the pointwise product on the axis, is the unique discrete analytic extension of it, and is commutative.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 6.2
nodes.statement: \mbox{}\\ $(1)$ Setting $y=0$ in \eqref{ckdef} and taking into account the definition of $\mathcal{Z}$ we have \[ \begin{split} (g\odot f)(x,0)&=c_0g(x,0)+c_1(\mathcal{Z} g)(x,0)+\dots+c_n(\mathcal{Z}^ng)(x,0)\\ &=c_0g(x,0)+c_1xg(x,0)+\cdots +c_nx^ng(x,0)\\ &=f(x,0)g(x,0). \end{split} \] $(2)$ For an expandable function the discrete Cauchy-Riemann equation $\overline{D}f=0$ with prescribed initial values on the horizontal positive axis has a unique solution (see Theorem \ref{p52}).\\ $(3)$ is then clear from $(1)$ and $(2)$.

nodes.name: Origin of the name Cauchy-Kovalevskaya product
nodes.statement: Recall that the classical Cauchy-Kovalevskaya theorem concerns uniqueness of solutions of certain partial differential equations with given initial conditions. See for instance \cite{MR93j:26013}. In Clifford analysis, where the pointwise product of hyperholomorphic functions need not be hyperholomorphic, this theorem was used by F. Sommen in \cite{MR618518} (see also \cite{bds}) to define the product of hyperholomorphic quaternionic-valued functions in $\mathbb R^4$ by extending the pointwise product from an hyperplane. In the present setting of expandable functions the discrete Cauchy-Riemann equation $\overline{D}f=0$ with prescribed initial values on the horizontal positive axis also has a unique solution. This is why the pointwise product on the horizontal positive axis can be extended to a unique expandable function, which we call the C-K product.
nodes.section: 6 The Cauchy-Kovalevskaya product
nodes.statement_short: As in Clifford analysis (Sommen), uniqueness for the discrete Cauchy-Riemann initial value problem lets the axis product extend uniquely.

Indeed, \[ e_{x,0}(t)=(1+t)^x \] is the restriction of an expandable function whenever $|t|<\sqrt{2}$. On the other hand, $(e_{x,0}(t))^2=e_{x,0}(2t+t^2)$ will not be the restriction of an expandable function for $|t|>\sqrt{1+\sqrt{2}}-1$ which is strictly smaller than $\sqrt{2}$.

nodes.name: Rational expandable functions are C-K quotients of polynomials
nodes.statement: An expandable function $f:\mathbb{Z}_+\times\mathbb{Z}\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}$ is rational if and only if it is a C-K quotient of discrete analytic polynomials function that is, if and only if there exist discrete analytic polynomials $p(x,y)$ and $q(x,y)$ such that $$\forall x\in\mathbb{Z}_+,\qquad q(x,0)\not=0$$ and $$(q\odot f)(x,y)\equiv p(x,y).$$

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 7.6
nodes.statement: Suppose first that $f$ is rational, and let $f_0(x)$ denote the restriction of $f$ to the horizontal positive axis. By definition there exists two polynomials $p_0(x)$ and $q_0(x)$ such that $q_0(x)\not=0$ (on $\mathbb{Z}_+$) and \[ q_0(x)f_0(x)=p_0(x),\quad x\in\mathbb{Z}_+. \] Let $p(x,y)$ and $q(x,y)$ denote the discrete analytic polynomials extending $p_0(x)$ and $q_0(x)$ respectively. Then both $p$ and $q\odot f$ are expandable functions, which coincide on $\mathbb{Z}_+$, and therefore everywhere.\\ Conversely, let $p(x,y)$ and $q(x,y)$ be the discrete analytic polynomials such that $$\forall x\in\mathbb{Z}_+,\qquad q(x,0)\not=0$$and $$(q\odot f)(x,y)\equiv p(x,y).$$ Setting $y=0$ leads to $$\forall x\in\mathbb{Z}_+,\quad q(x,0)f(x,0)=p(x,0),$$ which ends the proof.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 7.7
nodes.statement: Denote $$g(x,y)=(q\odot f)(x,y).$$ According to Proposition \ref{ok2}, the function $g:\mathbb{Z}_+\times\mathbb{Z}\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}$ is expandable, and therefore can be written as $$g(x,y)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}_+}\hat{g_0}(n)\zeta_n(x,y),$$ where $\hat{g_0}$ is the Fourier transform of its restriction $$g_0(x)=g(x,0).$$ In particular, by Theorem \ref{p52}, $g$ is discrete analytic. In view of Theorem \ref{t1}, $$g(x,y)\equiv p(x,y).$$

nodes.name: Lozenge inverse of I - zA is the exponential
nodes.statement: Let $\mathcal{H}$ be a Hilbert space and let $A$ is a bounded operator from $\mathcal{H}$ into itself. Then the $\mathbf L(\mathcal{H})$-valued entire function $$(I_{\mathcal{H}}-zA)^{-{\lozenge}}=(\sum_{n=0}^\infty\dfrac{ z^{n}A^n}{n!})=e^{zA}$$ satisfies \[ (I_{\mathcal{H}}-zA){\lozenge} (I_{\mathcal{H}}-zA)^{-{\lozenge}}=I_{\mathcal{H}}, \] and it is the only function in $T\mathcal{O}$ with this property.

nodes.name: Hardy space H_2
nodes.statement: Take now $\mathcal{H}=\mathbb C$ and let $\mathbf H_2$ denote the Hardy space of the unit disk.

nodes.name: T is a positive contractive injection on H_2
nodes.statement: Then $T$ is a positive contractive injection from $\mathbf H_2$ into itself.

nodes.name: Space bold H
nodes.statement: Denote by $\mathbf{H}$ the space $T\mathbf{H}_2$ equipped with the range norm: $$\forall f\in\mathbf{H}_2, \qquad \|Tf\|_\mathbf{H}=\|f\|_2.$$

nodes.name: bold H is a RKHS of entire functions
nodes.statement: Then $T:\mathbf{H}_2\longrightarrow \mathbf{H}$ is unitary, and $\mathbf{H}$ is a reproducing kernel Hilbert space of entire functions with the reproducing kernel $$K_{\mathbf{H}}(z,w)=\sum_{n=0}^\infty\dfrac{(zw^*)^n}{(n!)^2}.$$
nodes.section: 9 A reproducing kernel Hilbert space of entire functions
nodes.statement_short: $T$ is unitary onto $\mathbf H$, a RKHS of entire functions with kernel $\sum (zw^*)^n/(n!)^2$.

nodes.name: Integral characterization of bold H via Bessel K_0
nodes.statement: $\mathbf{H}$ is the Hilbert space of entire functions such that $$\int_\mathbb{C}|f(z)|^2K_0(2|z|)dA(z)<\infty,$$ where $$K_0(r)=\dfrac{1}{\pi}\int_\mathbb{R}\exp(-r\cosh t)dt$$ is the modified Bessel function of the second kind of order $0$.
nodes.section: 9 A reproducing kernel Hilbert space of entire functions
nodes.statement_short: $\mathbf H$ consists of entire $f$ with $\int|f|^2K_0(2|z|)dA<\infty$.

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 9.2
nodes.statement: This follows from the fact that the Mellin transform of the square of the function $\Gamma$ is the function $K_0(2\sqrt{x})$. See for instance \cite[p. 50]{colombo} for the latter.
nodes.section: 9 A reproducing kernel Hilbert space of entire functions
nodes.statement_short: Mellin transform of $\Gamma^2$ is $K_0(2\sqrt x)$.

nodes.name: bold H is contractively included in the Fock space
nodes.statement: We note that $\mathbf{H}$ is contractively included in the Fock space since the reproducing kernel of the latter is \[ K_F(z,w)=\sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{z^nw^{*n}}{n!}, \] and \[ K_F(z,w)-K_{\mathbf{H}}(z,w)=\sum_{n=0}^\infty(zw^*)^n\left( \frac{1}{n!}- \frac{1}{(n!)^2}\right) \] is positive definite in $\mathbb C$.

nodes.name: Pointwise multipliers of bold H are constants
nodes.statement: In view of Liouville's theorem, the only multipliers on $\mathbf{H}$ in the sense of the usual pointwise product are constants.

nodes.name: Contractive lozenge-multipliers of bold H
nodes.statement: A function $s\in\mathcal{O}$ is a contractive ${\lozenge}$-multiplier on $\mathbf{H}$ if and only if it is of the form $$s=Ts_0,\quad s_0\in\mathscr{S},$$ where $\mathscr{S}$ denotes the Schur class of functions analytic and contractive in the open unit disk.
nodes.section: 9 A reproducing kernel Hilbert space of entire functions
nodes.statement_short: Contractive $\lozenge$-multipliers of $\mathbf H$ are exactly $Ts_0$ with $s_0$ in the Schur class.
conclusions: if and only if it is of the form $$s=Ts_0,\quad s_0\in\mathscr{S},$$

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 9.3
nodes.statement: Assume first that $s\in\mathcal{O}$ is a contractive ${\lozenge}$-multiplier on $\mathbf{H}$. Then $s=s\lozenge1\in\mathbf{H}$ and hence $s=Ts_0$ for some $s_0\in\mathbf{H}_2$. Furthermore, let $f\in\mathbf{H}_2$. Since $s\lozenge(Tf)=T(s_0f)\in\mathbf{H}$, $s_0f\in\mathbf{H}_2.$ Since $$\|f\|_{\mathbf{H}_2}=\|Tf\|_\mathbf{H}\geq\|s\lozenge(Tf)\|_\mathbf{H}=\|T(s_0f)\|_\mathbf{H}=\|s_0f\|_{\mathbf{H}_2},$$ $s_0\in\mathscr{S}.$ Conversely, if $s=Ts_0$ where $s_0\in\mathscr{S}$, and $f\in\mathbf{H}_2$ then $s\lozenge(Tf)=T(s_0f)\in\mathbf{H}$ and $$\|s\lozenge(Tf)\|_\mathbf{H}=\|T(s_0f)\|_\mathbf{H}=\|s_0f\|_{\mathbf{H}_2} \leq\|f\|_{\mathbf{H}_2}=\|Tf\|_\mathbf{H}.$$ Thus $s$ is a contractive ${\lozenge}$-multiplier on $\mathbf{H}$.
nodes.section: 9 A reproducing kernel Hilbert space of entire functions
nodes.statement_short: Transfer via the unitary $T$: $s\lozenge Tf=T(s_0f)$, so contractivity of one is that of the other.

nodes.name: Pointwise multiplication operator M_{s_0}
nodes.statement: Let $s_0\in\mathscr S$. The operator $M_{s_0}$ of pointwise multiplication is a contraction from $\mathbf{H}_2$ into itself.

nodes.name: de Branges-Rovnyak space H(s_0)
nodes.statement: The operator range $\sqrt{I-M_{s_0}M_{s_0}^*}$ endowed with the range norm is called the associated de Branges-Rovnyak space. We denote it by $H(s_0)$.

nodes.name: Kernel K_s and lozenge-multiplication M_s
nodes.statement: Similarly one can associate with $s\in T\mathscr{S}$ a reproducing kernel $$K_s(z,w)=\left((I-M_sM_s^*)K_\mathbf{H}(\cdot,w)\right)(z),$$ where $M_s$ denotes the operator of ${\lozenge}$-multiplication by $s$ on $\mathbf{H}$.
nodes.section: 9 A reproducing kernel Hilbert space of entire functions

nodes.name: Space H(s)
nodes.statement: The corresponding reproducing kernel Hilbert space is $\mathrm{ran}(\sqrt{I-M_sM_s^*})$ with the range norm; it will be denoted by $H(s)$.
nodes.section: 9 A reproducing kernel Hilbert space of entire functions

nodes.name: T maps H(s_0) unitarily onto H(s)
nodes.statement: The mapping $f\mapsto Tf$ is unitary from de Branges - Rovnyak space $H(s_0)$ onto $H(s)$.
nodes.section: 9 A reproducing kernel Hilbert space of entire functions
conclusions: The mapping $f\mapsto Tf$ is unitary from de Branges - Rovnyak space $H(s_0)$ onto $H(s)$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 9.4
nodes.statement: Since $$M_sT=TM_{s_0},$$ $$\sqrt{I-M_sM_s^*}T=T\sqrt{I-M_{s_0}M_{s_0}^*}.$$
nodes.section: 9 A reproducing kernel Hilbert space of entire functions
nodes.statement_short: Intertwining $M_sT=TM_{s_0}$ passes to the square roots of the defect operators.

nodes.name: Differentiation operator
nodes.statement: The $H(s)$ spaces can be characterized in terms of $\partial$-invariance, where $\partial$ is the differentiation operator: $$\partial f = f^\prime.$$
nodes.section: 9 A reproducing kernel Hilbert space of entire functions

nodes.name: Differentiation on bold H
nodes.statement: The operator $\partial$ is bounded on $\mathbf{H}$; moreover, \begin{equation} \partial T=TR_0, \end{equation} where $R_0$ is the backward shift operator, and $$\partial^*\partial=I_\mathbf{H}-C^*C,\quad \partial\partial^*=I_\mathbf{H},$$ where $Cf:=f(0)$. Furthermore, the reproducing kernel of $\mathbf{H}$ is given by $$K_\mathbf{H}(z,w)=Ce^{z\partial}e^{w^*\partial^*}C^*.$$
nodes.section: 9 A reproducing kernel Hilbert space of entire functions
nodes.statement_short: $\partial$ is bounded on $\mathbf H$, $\partial T=TR_0$, $\partial\partial^*=I$, and $K_{\mathbf H}=Ce^{z\partial}e^{w^*\partial^*}C^*$.

nodes.name: Intertwining of d/dz and backward shift
nodes.statement: \partial T=TR_0,

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 9.5
nodes.statement: The claims follow from the definition of the operator $T$ in \eqref{opeT}. We prove only \eqref{r0}. Let $f\in\mathbf H_2$ with power series expansion \[ f(z)=\sum_{n=0}^\infty a_nz^n. \] Then, \[ (R_0f)(z)=\sum_{n=1}^\infty a_nz^{n-1}, \] and therefore \[ \begin{split} (TR_0f)(z)&=\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{a_n}{(n-1)!}z^{n-1}\\ &=\frac{d}{dz}\left(\sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{a_n}{n!}z^n\right)\\ &=(\partial Tf)(z). \end{split} \]

nodes.statement_short: From the definition of $T$; only $\partial T=TR_0$ is checked, on power series.

nodes.name: Beurling-Lax theorem for bold H
nodes.statement: A closed subspace $H$ of $\mathbf{H}$ is $\partial$-invariant if and only if $$H=\mathbf{H}\ominus M_{Ts_0}\mathbf{H},$$ where $s_0(z)$ is an inner function.
nodes.section: 9 A reproducing kernel Hilbert space of entire functions
nodes.statement_short: Closed $\partial$-invariant subspaces of $\mathbf H$ are $\mathbf H\ominus M_{Ts_0}\mathbf H$ with $s_0$ inner.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 9.6
nodes.statement: Let $H$ be a closed subspace of $\mathbf{H}$ then $H=TH_0$ where $H_0$ is a closed subspace of $\mathbf{H}_2$. $H$ is $\partial$-invariant if and only if $H_0$ is $R_0$-invariant, which is equivalent to $\mathbf{H}_2\ominus H_0$ being invariant under multiplication by $z$. By the Beurling-Lax theorem, the last condition holds if and only if $\mathbf{H}_2\ominus H_0=M_{s_0}\mathbf{H}_2,$ where $s_0$ is an inner function.
nodes.section: 9 A reproducing kernel Hilbert space of entire functions
nodes.statement_short: Transfer to $\mathbf H_2$ via $T$ and apply the classical Beurling-Lax theorem.

nodes.name: Realization of elements of T S
nodes.statement: Let $s\in T\mathscr{S}$. Then $s$ admits the representation $$s(z)=D+\int_0^zCe^{t\partial}Bdt,$$ where $$\begin{pmatrix} \partial & B\\ C& D\end{pmatrix}:\begin{pmatrix} H(s)\\ \mathbb{C}\end{pmatrix}\longrightarrow \begin{pmatrix} H(s)\\ \mathbb{C}\end{pmatrix}$$ is a coisometry given by \[ \nonumber \begin{split} \partial f&=f^\prime,\\ B1&=s^\prime,\\ Cf&=f(0),\\ D1&=s(0). \end{split} \]
nodes.section: 9 A reproducing kernel Hilbert space of entire functions
nodes.statement_short: Each $s\in T\mathscr S$ is $D+\int_0^zCe^{t\partial}B\,dt$ for a coisometric colligation on $H(s)$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 9.7
nodes.statement: Write $s=Ts_0$, where $s_0\in\mathscr{S}$. Then $$s_0(z)=D_0+zC_0(I-zR_0)^{-1}B_0,$$ where $$\begin{pmatrix} R_0 & B_0\\ C_0& D_0\end{pmatrix}:\begin{pmatrix} H(s_0)\\ \mathbb{C}\end{pmatrix}\longrightarrow \begin{pmatrix} H(s_0)\\ \mathbb{C}\end{pmatrix}$$ is a coisometry given by \[ \nonumber \begin{split} R_0 f&=(f-f(0))/z,\\ B_01&=R_0s_0,\\ C_0f&=f(0),\\ D_01&=s_0(0)=s(0). \end{split} \] Hence \[ \nonumber \begin{split} s(z)&=D_0+\sum_{n=0}^\infty \dfrac{z^{n+1}}{(n+1)!} C_0R_0^nB_0\\ &=D_0+\sum_{n=0}^\infty \dfrac{z^{n+1}}{(n+1)!}C_0T^{-1}(TR_0T^{-1})^nTB_0\\ &=D+\sum_{n=0}^\infty \dfrac{z^{n+1}}{(n+1)!}C\partial^nB\\ &= D+\int_0^zCe^{t\partial}Bdt. \end{split} \]
nodes.section: 9 A reproducing kernel Hilbert space of entire functions
nodes.statement_short: Take the de Branges-Rovnyak backward-shift realization of $s_0$ and conjugate by $T$.

nodes.name: Coisometric realizations give contractive lozenge-multipliers
nodes.statement: Let $H$ be a Hilbert space and let $$\begin{pmatrix}A&B\\C&D\end{pmatrix}:\begin{pmatrix}H\\ \mathbb{C} \end{pmatrix}\longrightarrow\begin{pmatrix}H\\ \mathbb{C}\end{pmatrix}$$ be a coisometry. Then the function $$s(z)=D+\int_0^zCe^{tA}Bdt$$ is a contractive ${\lozenge}$-multiplier on $\mathbf{H}$, and the corresponding reproducing kernel is given by $$K_s(z,w)=Ce^{zA}e^{w^*A^*}C^*.$$
nodes.section: 9 A reproducing kernel Hilbert space of entire functions
nodes.statement_short: For a coisometry $(A,B;C,D)$, $D+\int_0^zCe^{tA}B\,dt$ is a contractive $\lozenge$-multiplier with kernel $Ce^{zA}e^{w^*A^*}C^*$.
assumptions: Let $H$ be a Hilbert space and let $$\begin{pmatrix}A&B\\C&D\end{pmatrix}:\begin{pmatrix}H\\ \mathbb{C} \end{pmatrix}\longrightarrow\begin{pmatrix}H\\ \mathbb{C}\end{pmatrix}$$ be a coisometry.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 9.8
nodes.statement: Set $$s_0(z)=D+zC(I-zA)^{-1}B,$$ then $s_0\in\mathscr{S}$ and $s=Ts_0$. Since $$K_{s_0}(z,w)=C(I-zA)^{-1}(I-wA)^{-*}C^*,$$ the formula for $K_s(z,w)$ follows.
nodes.section: 9 A reproducing kernel Hilbert space of entire functions
nodes.statement_short: $s=Ts_0$ with $s_0$ the classical transfer function of the coisometry.

nodes.name: Characterization of H(s) spaces by delta-invariance
nodes.statement: A reproducing kernel Hilbert space $H$ of functions in $\mathcal{O}$ is of the form $H=H(s)$ for some $s\in T\mathscr{S}$ if and only if \begin{enumerate} \item $H$ is $\partial$-invariant; \item for every $f\in H$ $$\|\partial f\|_H^2\leq\|f\|_H^2-|f(0)|^2.$$ \end{enumerate}
nodes.section: 9 A reproducing kernel Hilbert space of entire functions
nodes.statement_short: A RKHS in $\mathcal O$ is some $H(s)$ iff it is $\partial$-invariant with $\|\partial f\|^2\le\|f\|^2-|f(0)|^2$.

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 9.9
nodes.statement: One direction follows immediately from Theorem \ref{s2}. The proof of the other direction is modelled after the proof of \cite[Theorem 3.1.2, p. 85]{adrs} and is done as follows: let $H$ be $\partial$-invariant; then for every $f\in H$ $$Ce^{z\partial}f=f(z),$$ where $Cf=f(0).$ Hence the reproducing kernel of $H$ is given by $$L_(z,w)=Ce^{z\partial}e^{w^*\partial^*}C^*.$$ Since $$\partial^*\partial+C^*C\leq I,$$ there exists a coisometry $$\begin{pmatrix} \partial & B\\ C& D\end{pmatrix}:\begin{pmatrix} H\\ \mathbb{C}\end{pmatrix}\longrightarrow \begin{pmatrix} H\\ \mathbb{C}\end{pmatrix}.$$ But the the function $$s(z)=D+\int_0^zCe^{t\partial}Bdt$$ is a contractive ${\lozenge}$-multiplier and the associated kernel $K_s(z,w)$ coincides with $L(z,w)$. Hence $H=H(s).$
nodes.section: 9 A reproducing kernel Hilbert space of entire functions
nodes.statement_short: One direction from Theorem 9.4; conversely build a coisometric colligation with $\partial$ as main operator and compare kernels.

nodes.name: Characterization of lozenge-rational functions
nodes.statement: Tne following are equivalent: \begin{enumerate} \item A function $f\in T\mathcal{O}$ is ${\lozenge}$-rational in the sense that for some polynomial $p(z)$, not vanishing at the origin, $p{\lozenge} f$ is also a polynomial. \item $f(z)$ is of the form $$f(z)=D+\int_0^zCe^{tA}Bdt$$ with $A,B,C,D$ - matrices of suitable dimensions; \item the columns of $\partial f$ belong to a finite-dimensional $\partial$-invariant space. \end{enumerate}
nodes.section: 9 A reproducing kernel Hilbert space of entire functions
nodes.statement_short: $\lozenge$-rationality, an exponential realization with matrices, and finite-dimensional $\partial$-invariance are equivalent.
nodes.label: s5

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 9.10
nodes.statement: It suffices to observe that a function $f\in T\mathcal{O}$ is ${\lozenge}$- rational if and only if it is of the form $f=Tf_0$ where$f_0\in\mathcal{O}$ is rational in the usual sense.

nodes.statement_short: Reduce to $f=Tf_0$ with $f_0$ rational in the usual sense.

nodes.name: Product boxdot of expandable functions

Then $s$ admits the representation $$s(x,y)=D+Ce_{x,y}(\delta_x)\boxdot (\zeta_1(x,y)B),$$ where $$\begin{pmatrix} \delta_x & B\\ C& D\end{pmatrix}: \begin{pmatrix} H(s)\\ \mathbb{C}\end{pmatrix}\longrightarrow \begin{pmatrix} H(s)\\ \mathbb{C}\end{pmatrix}$$ is a coisometry given by \[ \nonumber \begin{split} B1&=s^\prime,\\ Cf&=f(0),\\ D1&=s(0). \end{split} \]

nodes.name: Uniqueness via the difference identity
nodes.statement: To show the uniqueness of $\hat f(n)$, assume that \eqref{tay} holds for some function $\hat f(n)$ and apply the identity \[ \delta x^{[n]}=nx^{[n-1]}\] repeatedly to obtain \eqref{fou1}.
nodes.section: 2 Polynomials and rational functions on the set of integers
nodes.statement_short: Uniqueness: apply $\delta x^{[n]}=nx^{[n-1]}$ repeatedly to recover the coefficients.

nodes.name: Define the candidate series
nodes.statement: Next, let the function $\hat f(n)$ be defined by \eqref{fou1}. Then, according to Proposition \ref{tay1}, the series $$\tilde f(x):=\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}_+} \hat f(n)x^{[n]}$$ converges absolutely for every $x\in\mathbb{Z}_+$ and defines a function $\tilde f:\mathbb{Z}_+\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}.$
nodes.section: 2 Polynomials and rational functions on the set of integers
nodes.statement_short: Define $\hat f$ by the formula and the series $\tilde f$, finite by Proposition 2.2.

nodes.name: Matching differences at 0
nodes.statement: Hence \eqref{fou1} holds with $\tilde f$ replacing $f$ and $$\forall n\in\mathbb{Z}_+,\qquad (\delta^nf)(0)=n! \hat f(n)=(\delta^n\tilde f)(0).$$
nodes.section: 2 Polynomials and rational functions on the set of integers
nodes.statement_short: All differences of $f$ and $\tilde f$ agree at the origin.

nodes.name: Induction on x
nodes.statement: Now one can verify that \[ \forall x\in\mathbb{Z}_+,\,\,\forall n\in\mathbb{Z}_+,\qquad (\delta^nf)(x)=(\delta^n\tilde f)(x) \] by induction on $x$: If $$ \forall n\in\mathbb{Z}_+, \qquad (\delta^nf)(x)=(\delta^n\tilde f)(x)$$ then \begin{multline*} \forall n\in\mathbb{Z}_+, \qquad (\delta^nf)(x+1)=(\delta^nf)(x)+(\delta^{n+1}f)(x)\\= (\delta^n\tilde f)(x)+(\delta^{n+1}\tilde f)(x) =(\delta^n\tilde f)(x+1).\end{multline*}
nodes.section: 2 Polynomials and rational functions on the set of integers
nodes.statement_short: Induction on $x$ shows all differences agree everywhere.

nodes.name: Conclude with n = 0
nodes.statement: It remains to set $n=0$ in \eqref{hu1} to obtain \eqref{tay}.
