nodes.statement_short: Set $n=0$ to get the expansion.

nodes.name: Differencing lowers degree
nodes.statement: Note that $$\deg(\delta f)=\deg(f)-1$$ (if $f=\mathrm{const},$ $\delta f=0$). Hence $$\forall n\in\mathbb{Z}_+,\qquad n>\deg(f)\Longrightarrow \delta^nf=0.$$
nodes.section: 2 Polynomials and rational functions on the set of integers
nodes.statement_short: Each difference lowers the degree, so high-order differences vanish.

nodes.name: Vanishing of high coefficients
nodes.statement: Since $$(\delta f)_{|_{\mathbb{Z}_+}}=\delta(f_{|_{\mathbb{Z}_+}}),$$ \eqref{fou1} implies that $$\forall n>\deg(f),\qquad \hat f(n)=0.$$
nodes.section: 2 Polynomials and rational functions on the set of integers
nodes.statement_short: By the coefficient formula the transform vanishes beyond $\deg f$.

nodes.name: Polynomial identity extends to Z
nodes.statement: It follows that $$\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}_+}\hat f(n)x^{[n]}$$ is, in fact, a polynomial, which coincides with the polynomial $f(x)$ on $\mathbb{Z}_+$ and hence on $\mathbb{Z}$.
nodes.section: 2 Polynomials and rational functions on the set of integers
nodes.statement_short: The finite series is a polynomial agreeing with $f$ on $\mathbb{Z}_+$, hence on $\mathbb{Z}$.

nodes.name: Recall realization of rational functions
nodes.statement: We first recall that a matrix-valued rational function of a complex variable can always be written in the form \[ r(z)=p(z)+C(zI-A)^{-1}B, \] where the matrix-valued polynomial $p$ takes care of the pole at infinity, and $A,B$ and $C$ are matrices of appropriate sizes. Furthermore, when the dimension of $A$ is minimal, the (finite) poles of $r$ coincide with the spectrum of $A$; see \cite{bgk1, MR0255260}. Here, we consider complex-valued functions, and thus $C$ and $B$ are respectively a row and column vector.
nodes.section: 2 Polynomials and rational functions on the set of integers
nodes.statement_short: Recall the state-space realization of rational matrix functions.

nodes.name: Restriction to Z_+
nodes.statement: Now, by Definition \ref{defrat1}, $f$ is a rational function if and only if it is the restriction on $\mathbb{Z}_+$ of a rational function of a complex variable, with no poles on $\mathbb{Z}_+$, that is if and only if it can be written as \eqref{eqreal} with the matrix $A$ satisfying furthermore \eqref{kaas}.
nodes.section: 2 Polynomials and rational functions on the set of integers
nodes.statement_short: Rational on $\mathbb{Z}_+$ means restriction of a rational function without poles on $\mathbb{Z}_+$.

nodes.name: Realize f
nodes.statement: According to Proposition \ref{ABC}, there exist a polynomial $p(x)$ and matrices $A,B,C$ such that $\sigma(A)\cap\mathbb{Z}_+=\emptyset$ and $$f(x)=p(x)+C(xI-A)^{-1}B.$$
nodes.section: 2 Polynomials and rational functions on the set of integers
nodes.statement_short: Write $f$ via the realization of Proposition 2.8.

nodes.name: Bound the differences
nodes.statement: Hence, for $n>\deg(p)$, $$|\hat{f}(n)n!|=|(\delta^nf)(0)|\leq\|C\|\cdot\|B\|\cdot\|A^{-1}\|\cdot \prod_{j=1}^n\|\left(I-\dfrac{1}{n}A\right)^{-1}\|.$$
nodes.section: 2 Polynomials and rational functions on the set of integers
nodes.statement_short: Bound $|(\delta^nf)(0)|$ by a product of resolvent norms.

nodes.name: Limit of resolvent norms
nodes.statement: Since $$\lim_{n\rightarrow\infty}\|\left(I-\dfrac{1}{n}A\right)^{-1}\|=1,$$ $$\forall\epsilon>0,\,\,\exists M,N\in\mathbb{Z}_+,\,\forall n\in\mathbb{Z}_+\quad:\quad n\geq N\Longrightarrow|\hat{f}(n)n!|\leq M(1+\epsilon)^n,$$ and the conclusion follows.
nodes.section: 2 Polynomials and rational functions on the set of integers
nodes.statement_short: Resolvent norms tend to 1, giving the $\limsup$ bound.

nodes.name: Expand in y for fixed x
nodes.statement: First, fix $x\in\mathbb{Z}_+$ and consider the function $f_x:\mathbb{Z}_+\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}$ given by $$f_x(y)=f(x,y),\quad y\in\mathbb{Z}_+.$$ Then, according to Proposition \ref{tay2}, there is a unique function $\hat{ f_x}:\mathbb{Z}_+\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}$ such that $$\forall y\in\mathbb{Z}_+,\qquad f_x(y)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}_+}\hat{f_x}(n) y^{[n]};$$ the function $\hat{f_x}(n)$ is given by $$\hat{f_x}(n)=\dfrac{(\delta_y^n f)(x,0)}{n!},\quad n\in\mathbb{Z}_+.$$
nodes.section: 3 Discrete polynomials of two variables
nodes.statement_short: Apply Proposition 2.3 to $y\mapsto f(x,y)$.

nodes.name: Expand the coefficients in x
nodes.statement: Next, fix $n\in\mathbb{Z}_+$ and consider the function $g_n:\mathbb{Z}_+\longrightarrow \mathbb{C}$ given by $$g_n(x)=\hat{f_x}(n),\quad x\in\mathbb{Z}_+.$$ By the same Proposition \ref{tay2}, there is a unique function $\hat{g_n}:\mathbb{Z}_+\longrightarrow \mathbb{C}$ such that $$\forall x\in\mathbb{Z}_+,\qquad g_n(x)=\sum_{m\in\mathbb{Z}_+}\hat{g_n}(m) x^{[m]};$$ the function $\hat{g_n}(m)$ is given by $$\hat{g_n}(m)=\dfrac{(\delta_x^m\delta_y^n f)(0,0)}{m!n!},\quad m\in\mathbb{Z}_+.$$
nodes.section: 3 Discrete polynomials of two variables
nodes.statement_short: Apply Proposition 2.3 again to each coefficient as a function of $x$.

nodes.name: Combine expansions
nodes.statement: Thus $$\forall (x,y)\in\mathbb{Z}_+^2,\qquad f(x,y)=\sum_{(m,n) \in\mathbb{Z}_+^2}\hat{g_n}(m) x^{[m]}y^{[n]}.$$ It remains to set $\hat f(m,n)=\hat{g_n}(m).$
nodes.section: 3 Discrete polynomials of two variables
nodes.statement_short: Combine into the double expansion.

nodes.name: Expand f and g
nodes.statement: By Proposition \ref{p11}, there exist functions $\hat f,\hat g:\mathbb{Z}_+^2\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}$ with finite support, such that $$f(x,y)=\sum_{(m,n)\in\mathbb{Z}_+^2}\hat{f}(m,n)x^{[m]}y^{[n]},\quad g(x,y)=\sum_{(m,n)\in\mathbb{Z}_+^2}\hat{g}(m,n)x^{[m]}y^{[n]}.$$
nodes.section: 3 Discrete polynomials of two variables
nodes.statement_short: Expand $f,g$ in finite double Newton series.

nodes.name: Coefficient relation
nodes.statement: Then identity \eqref{co01} implies that \[ \forall (m,n)\in\mathbb{Z}^2_+,\qquad (n+1)\hat{f}(m,n+1)=(m+1)\hat{g}(m+1,n).\]
nodes.section: 3 Discrete polynomials of two variables
nodes.statement_short: The compatibility condition gives a relation between coefficients.

nodes.name: Construct h
nodes.statement: Consider the polynomial $$h(x,y)=\sum_{(m,n)\in\mathbb{Z}_+^2}\dfrac{\hat{f}(m,n)}{m+1} x^{[m+1]}y^{[n]}+\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}_+}\dfrac{\hat{g}(0,n)}{n+1}y^{[n+1]},$$ then $$\forall (x,y)\in\mathbb{Z}^2,\qquad(\delta_x h)(x,y)=\sum_{(m,n)\in\mathbb{Z}_+^2}\hat{f}(m,n) x^{[m]}y^{[n]}=f(x,y).$$
nodes.section: 3 Discrete polynomials of two variables
nodes.statement_short: Define $h$ explicitly; then $\delta_xh=f$.

nodes.name: Check delta_y h = g
nodes.statement: On the other hand, in view of \eqref{use03}, $$h(x,y)=\sum_{(m,n)\in\mathbb{Z}_+^2}\dfrac{\hat{g}(m,n)}{n+1} x^{[m]}y^{[n+1]}+\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}_+}\dfrac{\hat{f}(m,0)}{m+1}x^{[m+1]},$$ hence $$\forall (x,y)\in\mathbb{Z}^2,\qquad(\delta_y h)(x,y)=\sum_{(m,n)\in\mathbb{Z}_+^2}\hat{g}(m,n) x^{[m]}y^{[n]}=g(x,y).$$
nodes.section: 3 Discrete polynomials of two variables
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite $h$ using the coefficient relation to get $\delta_yh=g$.

nodes.name: Minimal counterexample
nodes.statement: Assume the opposite, then $\deg(q)>0,$ and $q$ can be chosen so that $\deg q$ is the smallest possible.
nodes.section: 4 Discrete analytic polynomials
nodes.statement_short: Assume a nonzero such $q$ of minimal degree.

nodes.name: delta_x q vanishes
nodes.statement: Observe that $(\delta_xq)(x,y)$ is also a discrete analytic polynomial, that $ (\delta_xq)(x,0)\equiv 0,$ and that $\deg(\delta_xp)<\deg(p).$ Hence $(\delta_xq)(x,y)\equiv 0.$
nodes.section: 4 Discrete analytic polynomials
nodes.statement_short: $\delta_xq$ is a smaller counterexample candidate, so it vanishes.

nodes.name: delta_y q vanishes
nodes.statement: Since $q(x,y)$ is discrete analytic, Definition \ref{maindef2} implies that $$\forall (x,y)\in\mathbb{Z}^2,\qquad (\delta_yq)(x,y)= \dfrac{i-1}{2}((1-i+\delta_y)\delta_xq)(x,y)= 0.$$
nodes.section: 4 Discrete analytic polynomials
nodes.statement_short: The Cauchy-Riemann operator (Theorem 4.1) forces $\delta_yq=0$.

nodes.name: Contradiction
nodes.statement: Thus $$(\delta_xq)(x,y)\equiv(\delta_yq)(x,y)\equiv 0$$ and hence $q=\mathrm{const}$ - a contradiction.
nodes.section: 4 Discrete analytic polynomials
nodes.statement_short: So $q$ is constant, a contradiction.

nodes.name: Uniqueness from Lemma 4.3
nodes.statement: The uniqueness of the polynomial $q(x,y)$ follows from Lemma \ref{l1}.
nodes.section: 4 Discrete analytic polynomials
nodes.statement_short: Uniqueness follows from Lemma 4.3.

nodes.name: Base case: constant p
nodes.statement: The existence in the case $p=\mathrm{const}$ is clear: it suffices to set $$q(x,y)=p(0).$$
nodes.section: 4 Discrete analytic polynomials
nodes.statement_short: Base case: constant $p$.

nodes.name: Inductive step
nodes.statement: If $p\not=\mathrm{const}$ we proceed by induction on $d=\deg(p)$. According to Proposition \ref{p03}, $(\delta p)(x)$ is a polynomial and $\deg(\delta p)=d-1$. Therefore, by the induction assumption, there is a discrete analytic polynomial $f(x,y)$, such that $$\forall x\in\mathbb{Z},\qquad f(x,0)=(\delta p)(x)$$ and $\deg(f)=d-1.$ Let $g:\mathbb{Z}^2\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}$ be defined by $$g(x,y)=if(x,y)-\dfrac{1-i}{2}(\delta_yf)(x,y),$$ then $g(x,y)$ is also a discrete analytic polynomial, $\deg(g)=d-1.$ Furthermore, since $(\bar Df)(x,y)\equiv 0,$ \begin{multline*}\forall (x,y)\in\mathbb{Z}^2,\quad (\delta_xg)(x,y)=i(\delta_xf)(x,y)-\dfrac{1-i}{2}(\delta_x\delta_yf)(x,y)\\= i(\delta_xf)(x,y)+\dfrac{1-i}{2}((1-i)(\delta_xf)(x,y)+(1+i)(\delta_yf)(x,y))= (\delta_yf)(x,y).\end{multline*} Hence, according to Proposition \ref{p13}, there exists a polynomial $h:\mathbb{Z}^2\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}$ such that $$(\delta_xh)(x,y)\equiv f(x,y),\quad (\delta_y h)(x,y)\equiv g(x,y).$$ Since $$\forall (x,y)\in\mathbb{Z}^2,\qquad (\bar D h)(x,y)=(1-i)f(x,y)+(1+i)g(x,y)+(\delta_y f)(x,y)=0,$$ the polynomial $h(x,y)$ is discrete analytic. Finally, since $$\forall x\in\mathbb{Z},\qquad (\delta_x h)(x,0)=f(x,0)=(\delta p)(x),$$ $h(x,0)-p(x)$ is a constant function. Thus it suffices to set $$q(x,y)=h(x,y)-h(0,0)+p(0)$$ to complete the proof.
nodes.section: 4 Discrete analytic polynomials
nodes.statement_short: Inductive step on $d=\deg p$.

nodes.name: Extend delta p by induction
nodes.statement: If $p\not=\mathrm{const}$ we proceed by induction on $d=\deg(p)$. According to Proposition \ref{p03}, $(\delta p)(x)$ is a polynomial and $\deg(\delta p)=d-1$. Therefore, by the induction assumption, there is a discrete analytic polynomial $f(x,y)$, such that $$\forall x\in\mathbb{Z},\qquad f(x,0)=(\delta p)(x)$$ and $\deg(f)=d-1.$
nodes.section: 4 Discrete analytic polynomials
nodes.statement_short: By Proposition 2.6 and induction, extend $\delta p$ to a discrete analytic polynomial $f$.

nodes.name: Define g
nodes.statement: Let $g:\mathbb{Z}^2\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}$ be defined by $$g(x,y)=if(x,y)-\dfrac{1-i}{2}(\delta_yf)(x,y),$$ then $g(x,y)$ is also a discrete analytic polynomial, $\deg(g)=d-1.$ Furthermore, since $(\bar Df)(x,y)\equiv 0,$ \begin{multline*}\forall (x,y)\in\mathbb{Z}^2,\quad (\delta_xg)(x,y)=i(\delta_xf)(x,y)-\dfrac{1-i}{2}(\delta_x\delta_yf)(x,y)\\= i(\delta_xf)(x,y)+\dfrac{1-i}{2}((1-i)(\delta_xf)(x,y)+(1+i)(\delta_yf)(x,y))= (\delta_yf)(x,y).\end{multline*}
nodes.section: 4 Discrete analytic polynomials
nodes.statement_short: Define $g$ so that $\delta_xg=\delta_yf$.

nodes.name: Antidifference h
nodes.statement: Hence, according to Proposition \ref{p13}, there exists a polynomial $h:\mathbb{Z}^2\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}$ such that $$(\delta_xh)(x,y)\equiv f(x,y),\quad (\delta_y h)(x,y)\equiv g(x,y).$$ Since $$\forall (x,y)\in\mathbb{Z}^2,\qquad (\bar D h)(x,y)=(1-i)f(x,y)+(1+i)g(x,y)+(\delta_y f)(x,y)=0,$$ the polynomial $h(x,y)$ is discrete analytic.
nodes.section: 4 Discrete analytic polynomials
nodes.statement_short: Proposition 3.7 gives $h$ with $\delta_xh=f$, $\delta_yh=g$, which is discrete analytic.

nodes.name: Adjust constant
nodes.statement: Finally, since $$\forall x\in\mathbb{Z},\qquad (\delta_x h)(x,0)=f(x,0)=(\delta p)(x),$$ $h(x,0)-p(x)$ is a constant function. Thus it suffices to set $$q(x,y)=h(x,y)-h(0,0)+p(0)$$ to complete the proof.
nodes.section: 4 Discrete analytic polynomials
nodes.statement_short: $h(x,0)-p(x)$ is constant; shift $h$ to get $q$.

nodes.name: Taylor coefficients c_n
nodes.statement: The analyticity is clear because $x,y\in\mathbb{Z}$ and we have $$e_{x,y}(z)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}_+}\dfrac{z^n c_n(x,y)}{n!},\quad \forall z\in\mathbb{D}.$$ where $$c_n(x,y)=\dfrac{d^n}{dz^n}e_{x,y}\Bigm|_{z=0}.$$
nodes.section: 5 Expandable discrete analytic functions
nodes.statement_short: Introduce the Taylor coefficients $c_n$ of $e_{x,y}$.

nodes.name: Lowering identity for c_n
nodes.statement: Since $$e_{x+1,y}(z)-e_{x,y}(z)=ze_{x,y}(z)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}_+}\dfrac{z^{n+1} c_{n}(x,y)}{n!},$$ $$\forall (x,y)\in\mathbb{Z}^2,\,\,\forall n\in\mathbb{Z}_+,\qquad (\delta_xc_{n})(x,y)=nc_{n-1}(x,y)$$ (if $n=0,$ $c_0(x,y)\equiv 1$ and $(\delta_xc_0)(x,y)\equiv 0$).
nodes.section: 5 Expandable discrete analytic functions
nodes.statement_short: $\delta_xc_n=nc_{n-1}$.

nodes.name: c_n discrete analytic
nodes.statement: Similarly, since \[ \begin{split} \dfrac{e_{x+1,y+1}(z)-e_{x,y}(z)}{1+ i}-\dfrac{e_{x+1,y}(z)-e_{x,y+1}(z)}{1-i}&=\\ &\hspace{-5cm}=\left( (1+z)\dfrac{1+i+iz}{1+i+z}-1\right)\dfrac{e_{x,y}(z)}{1+i}-\left( 1+z-\dfrac{1+i+iz}{1+i+z}\right)\dfrac{e_{x,y}(z)}{1-i}\\ &\hspace{-5cm}=0, \end{split} \] we have $$\forall (x,y)\in\mathbb{Z}^2,\,\,{\rm and}\,\,\forall n\in\mathbb{Z}_+,\qquad (\bar Dc_{n})(x,y)=0.$$ Thus, for every $n\in\mathbb{Z}_+$, the function $c_n:\mathbb{Z}^2\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}$ is discrete analytic.
nodes.section: 5 Expandable discrete analytic functions
nodes.statement_short: The generating function satisfies the discrete Cauchy-Riemann equation, so each $c_n$ is discrete analytic.

nodes.name: Induction c_n = zeta_n
nodes.statement: Next, we show by induction that \[ \forall n\in\mathbb{Z}_+,\quad c_n(x,y)\equiv\zeta_n(x,y). \] Indeed, for $n=0$, $$c_0(x,y)\equiv 1\equiv\zeta_0(x,y).$$ Assume that, for some $n\in\mathbb{Z}_+$, $$c_n(x,y)\equiv\zeta_n(x,y),$$ then, in view of \eqref{hu3}, $$(\delta_xc_{n+1}(x,y)\equiv(n+1)c_n(x,y)\equiv (n+1)\zeta_n(x,y)\equiv(\delta_x\zeta_{n+1}(x,y),$$ hence $$(\delta_x(\zeta_{n+1}-c_{n+1}))(x,y)\equiv 0.$$ But the functions $c_{n+1}$ and $\zeta_{n+1}$ are discrete analytic, hence $$(\bar D(\zeta_{n+1}-c_{n+1}))(x,y)\equiv 0$$ and $$(\delta_y(\zeta_{n+1}-c_{n+1}))(x,y)\equiv 0.$$ It follows that $$\zeta_{n+1}-c_{n+1}=\mathrm{const};$$ since $$\zeta_{n+1}(0,0)=0=c_{n+1}(0,0),$$ one concludes that $$c_{n+1}(x,y)\equiv\zeta_{n+1}(x,y),$$ and \eqref{hu4} follows.
nodes.section: 5 Expandable discrete analytic functions
nodes.statement_short: Show $c_n=\zeta_n$ by induction.

nodes.name: Base case
nodes.statement: Indeed, for $n=0$, $$c_0(x,y)\equiv 1\equiv\zeta_0(x,y).$$
nodes.section: 5 Expandable discrete analytic functions
nodes.statement_short: Base case $n=0$.

nodes.name: Inductive step
nodes.statement: Assume that, for some $n\in\mathbb{Z}_+$, $$c_n(x,y)\equiv\zeta_n(x,y),$$ then, in view of \eqref{hu3}, $$(\delta_xc_{n+1}(x,y)\equiv(n+1)c_n(x,y)\equiv (n+1)\zeta_n(x,y)\equiv(\delta_x\zeta_{n+1}(x,y),$$ hence $$(\delta_x(\zeta_{n+1}-c_{n+1}))(x,y)\equiv 0.$$
nodes.section: 5 Expandable discrete analytic functions
nodes.statement_short: Lowering identities give $\delta_x(\zeta_{n+1}-c_{n+1})=0$.

nodes.name: delta_y difference vanishes
nodes.statement: But the functions $c_{n+1}$ and $\zeta_{n+1}$ are discrete analytic, hence $$(\bar D(\zeta_{n+1}-c_{n+1}))(x,y)\equiv 0$$ and $$(\delta_y(\zeta_{n+1}-c_{n+1}))(x,y)\equiv 0.$$
nodes.section: 5 Expandable discrete analytic functions
nodes.statement_short: Discrete analyticity gives $\delta_y(\zeta_{n+1}-c_{n+1})=0$.

nodes.name: Constant is zero
nodes.statement: It follows that $$\zeta_{n+1}-c_{n+1}=\mathrm{const};$$ since $$\zeta_{n+1}(0,0)=0=c_{n+1}(0,0),$$ one concludes that $$c_{n+1}(x,y)\equiv\zeta_{n+1}(x,y),$$ and \eqref{hu4} follows.
nodes.section: 5 Expandable discrete analytic functions
nodes.statement_short: The difference is constant and vanishes at the origin.

nodes.name: Set y = 0
nodes.statement: Set $y=0$ in $e_{x,y}(z)$ in \eqref{exy}. By \eqref{hu4} we get \[ (1+z)^x=\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}_+}\frac{z^n}{n!}\zeta_n(x,0). \]
nodes.section: 5 Expandable discrete analytic functions
nodes.statement_short: Set $y=0$ in the generating function.

nodes.name: Compare coefficients
nodes.statement: \eqref{value:zeta:n} follows by comparing the coefficients of $z^n$ in \eqref{eq:y=0}.
nodes.section: 5 Expandable discrete analytic functions
nodes.statement_short: Compare coefficients with the binomial series.

nodes.name: Z zeta_n is a discrete analytic polynomial
nodes.statement: By Proposition \ref{ok}, for every $n\in\mathbb{Z}_+$, $(\mathcal{Z}\zeta_n)(x,y)$ is a discrete analytic polynomial.
nodes.section: 7 Rational discrete analytic functions
nodes.statement_short: By Proposition 7.2, $\mathcal Z\zeta_n$ is a discrete analytic polynomial.

nodes.name: Identify Z zeta_n
nodes.statement: In view of \eqref{xmult}, $$(\mathcal{Z}\zeta_n)(x,0)= x\cdot x^{[n]}=x^{[n+1]}+n x^{[n]},$$ hence formula \eqref{hu5} follows from Theorem \ref{t1}.
nodes.section: 7 Rational discrete analytic functions
nodes.statement_short: Compare on the axis and use uniqueness (Theorem 4.2).

nodes.name: Expand Z f on the axis
nodes.statement: Let $f_0:\mathbb{Z}_+\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}$ be defined by \eqref{rest}, then $$(\mathcal{Z} f)(x,0)= xf_0(x)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}_+}(n\hat{f_0}(n)+\hat{f_0}(n-1))x^{[n]},$$ where $\hat{f_0}(-1):=0.$
nodes.section: 7 Rational discrete analytic functions
nodes.statement_short: Compute the Newton coefficients of $\mathcal Zf$ on the axis.

nodes.name: Growth estimate preserved
nodes.statement: Since $$\limsup_{n\rightarrow\infty}(|\hat{f_0}(n)|n!)^{1/n}<\sqrt{2},$$ $$\limsup_{n\rightarrow\infty}(|n\hat{f_0}(n)+\hat{f_0}(n-1)|n!)^{1/n}<\sqrt{2}.$$
nodes.section: 7 Rational discrete analytic functions
nodes.statement_short: The new coefficients satisfy the growth estimate.

nodes.name: Termwise application of Z
nodes.statement: Finally, since $$f(x,y)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}_+}\hat{f_0}(n)\zeta_n(x,y),$$ where the convergence is absolute, $$(\mathcal{Z} f)(x,y)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}_+}\hat{f_0}(n)(\mathcal{Z} \zeta_n)(x,y)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}_+}(n\hat{f_0}(n)+\hat{f_0}(n-1))\zeta_n(x,y).$$
nodes.section: 7 Rational discrete analytic functions
nodes.statement_short: Apply $\mathcal Z$ termwise to get the expansion of $\mathcal Zf$.

nodes.name: Rational implies C-K quotient
nodes.statement: Suppose first that $f$ is rational, and let $f_0(x)$ denote the restriction of $f$ to the horizontal positive axis. By definition there exists two polynomials $p_0(x)$ and $q_0(x)$ such that $q_0(x)\not=0$ (on $\mathbb{Z}_+$) and \[ q_0(x)f_0(x)=p_0(x),\quad x\in\mathbb{Z}_+. \] Let $p(x,y)$ and $q(x,y)$ denote the discrete analytic polynomials extending $p_0(x)$ and $q_0(x)$ respectively. Then both $p$ and $q\odot f$ are expandable functions, which coincide on $\mathbb{Z}_+$, and therefore everywhere.
nodes.section: 7 Rational discrete analytic functions
nodes.statement_short: If $f$ is rational, extend numerator and denominator and compare on the axis.

nodes.name: Converse
nodes.statement: Conversely, let $p(x,y)$ and $q(x,y)$ be the discrete analytic polynomials such that $$\forall x\in\mathbb{Z}_+,\qquad q(x,0)\not=0$$and $$(q\odot f)(x,y)\equiv p(x,y).$$ Setting $y=0$ leads to $$\forall x\in\mathbb{Z}_+,\quad q(x,0)f(x,0)=p(x,0),$$ which ends the proof.
nodes.section: 7 Rational discrete analytic functions
nodes.statement_short: Setting $y=0$ shows $f(x,0)$ is rational.

nodes.name: g is expandable
nodes.statement: Denote $$g(x,y)=(q\odot f)(x,y).$$ According to Proposition \ref{ok2}, the function $g:\mathbb{Z}_+\times\mathbb{Z}\longrightarrow\mathbb{C}$ is expandable, and therefore can be written as $$g(x,y)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}_+}\hat{g_0}(n)\zeta_n(x,y),$$ where $\hat{g_0}$ is the Fourier transform of its restriction $$g_0(x)=g(x,0).$$
nodes.section: 7 Rational discrete analytic functions
nodes.statement_short: By Proposition 7.3, $g=q\odot f$ is expandable.

nodes.name: g is discrete analytic
nodes.statement: In particular, by Theorem \ref{p52}, $g$ is discrete analytic.
nodes.section: 7 Rational discrete analytic functions
nodes.statement_short: By Theorem 5.4, $g$ is discrete analytic.

nodes.name: g is a polynomial
nodes.statement: In view of \eqref{xmult}, $$g_0(x)=q(x,0)f(x,0)=p(x,0),$$ hence, by Proposition \ref{p01}, $\hat{g_0}$ has finite support and $g$ is a discrete analytic polynomial.
nodes.section: 7 Rational discrete analytic functions
nodes.statement_short: Its axis restriction is $p(x,0)$, so by Proposition 2.5 $g$ is a polynomial.

nodes.name: g equals p
nodes.statement: In view of Theorem \ref{t1}, $$g(x,y)\equiv p(x,y).$$
nodes.section: 7 Rational discrete analytic functions
nodes.statement_short: Uniqueness of extension gives $g=p$.

nodes.name: Difference of generating function
nodes.statement: Using Proposition \ref{prop6.1}, we get \begin{equation} \delta_xe_{x,y}(z)=e_{x+1,y}(z)-e_{x,y}(z)=ze_{x,y}(z). \end{equation}
nodes.section: 8 The $C^*$-algebra associated to expandable discrete analytic functions
nodes.statement_short: From Proposition 5.1, $\delta_xe_{x,y}(z)=ze_{x,y}(z)$.

nodes.name: Compare coefficients
nodes.statement: Substituting the expression $e_{x,y}(z)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}_+}\frac{z^n}{n!}\zeta_n(x,y)$ into \eqref{eq1234}, we get $\delta_x\zeta_1=0$ and $\delta_x\zeta_n=n\zeta_{n-1}$ if $n>1$.
nodes.section: 8 The $C^*$-algebra associated to expandable discrete analytic functions
nodes.statement_short: Substitute the Taylor expansion to get $\delta_x\zeta_n=n\zeta_{n-1}$.

nodes.name: Normalize
nodes.statement: The result \eqref{copy:shift} follows.
nodes.section: 8 The $C^*$-algebra associated to expandable discrete analytic functions
nodes.statement_short: Normalize to $e_n$.

nodes.name: Recall D-bar
nodes.statement: Recall that the operator $\overline{\mathcal{D}}$ was defined in \eqref{COP}.
nodes.section: 8 The $C^*$-algebra associated to expandable discrete analytic functions
nodes.statement_short: Recall the operator $\bar{\mathcal D}$.

nodes.name: D-bar vanishes
nodes.statement: Since the elements of $\mathcal H_{DA}$ are discrete analytic we have $\overline{\mathcal{D}}=0$ in $\mathcal H_{DA}$, that is, \[ (1-i)\delta_x+(1+i)\delta_y+\delta_x\delta_y=0, \] and thus \[ \delta_y\left((1+i)I+\delta_x\right)=(1-i)\delta_x. \]
nodes.section: 8 The $C^*$-algebra associated to expandable discrete analytic functions
nodes.statement_short: Discrete analyticity gives $\bar{\mathcal D}=0$ on $\mathcal H_{DA}$.

nodes.name: Solve for delta_y
nodes.statement: Since $\delta_x$ is an isometry, and has in particular norm $1$, we can solve equation \eqref{deltay1} and obtain \eqref{deltay}.
nodes.section: 8 The $C^*$-algebra associated to expandable discrete analytic functions
nodes.statement_short: Solve for $\delta_y$ using $\|\delta_x\|=1$.

nodes.name: Norm convergence
nodes.statement: The power expansion converges in the operator norm since \[ \|\left(\frac{i-1}{2}\right)\delta_x\|=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}<1. \]
nodes.section: 8 The $C^*$-algebra associated to expandable discrete analytic functions
nodes.statement_short: The Neumann series converges in norm.

nodes.name: Reduction
nodes.statement: This follows from the preceding proposition and from \cite{MR0213906}.
nodes.section: 8 The $C^*$-algebra associated to expandable discrete analytic functions
nodes.statement_short: Reduce to Proposition 8.2 and Coburn.

nodes.name: Recall Coburn's theorem
nodes.statement: Indeed it is known \cite{MR0213906} that the Toeplitz $C^*$-algebra $\mathcal T$ is the unique $C^*$-algebra generated by the shift.
nodes.section: 8 The $C^*$-algebra associated to expandable discrete analytic functions
nodes.statement_short: Recall Coburn's theorem.

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: Since $\delta^*_x$ is a copy of the shift, and $\delta_y\in C^*(\delta^*_x)$, the result follows.
nodes.section: 8 The $C^*$-algebra associated to expandable discrete analytic functions
nodes.statement_short: $\delta_x^*$ is a shift and $\delta_y\in C^*(\delta_x^*)$.

nodes.name: Notation for the unitary group
nodes.statement: In $(iii)$, we denote by $e^{itA}$ the unitary one-parameter group generated by the self-adjoint operator $A$ from $(i)$.
nodes.section: 8 The $C^*$-algebra associated to expandable discrete analytic functions
nodes.statement_short: Fix notation $e^{itA}$.

nodes.name: Part (i)
nodes.statement: The matrix representation of $A$ with respect to the ONB $e_n:=\frac{1}{n!}\zeta_n$ is: \[ \begin{pmatrix} & & & & & & & &\\ & & & & 0 & & & &\\ & & &n-2&n-1&0& & &\\ & & &n-1&n-1&n&0& &\\ & & & &n &\boxed{n}&n+1&\\ & & & &0 &n+1&n+1&n+2\\ & & & &0&0&n+2&n+2\\ & & & & & &0&\\ \end{pmatrix} \] It is therefore a banded infinite matrix with terms going to infinity linearly with $n$. It follows from \cite{MR507913} that $A$ is essentially self-adjoint.
nodes.section: 8 The $C^*$-algebra associated to expandable discrete analytic functions
nodes.statement_short: Banded matrix with linearly growing entries is essentially self-adjoint (Jorgensen).

nodes.name: Part (ii)
nodes.statement: $(ii)$ By definition of $\mathcal{Z}$ and $\delta_x$ \[ \begin{split} [A,\delta_x^*](e_n)&=(A\delta_x^*-\delta_x^*A)(e_n)\\ &=\frac{1}{2}(e_n+e_{n+1}+e_{n+2})\\ &=\frac{1}{2}(I+\delta_x^*+\delta_x^{*2})e_n, \end{split} \] and hence the result.
nodes.section: 8 The $C^*$-algebra associated to expandable discrete analytic functions
nodes.statement_short: Compute the commutator on $e_n$.

nodes.name: Part (iii)
nodes.statement: $(iii)$ We have \begin{equation} e^{itA}be^{-itA}=\sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{(it)^n}{n!}\left({\rm ad}~A\right)^n (b), \end{equation} and \[ \left({\rm ad}~A\right)^{n+1} (b)=[A,\left({\rm ad}~A\right)^n b], \] We verify \eqref{sum} on monomials of $\delta_x$ and $\delta_x^*$ using \eqref{wert} and induction. See \cite{MR671318,MR548006} for more details regarding limits.
nodes.section: 8 The $C^*$-algebra associated to expandable discrete analytic functions
nodes.statement_short: Expand in iterated commutators and verify by induction.

nodes.name: Toeplitz extension
nodes.statement: By \cite{MR0213906}, the Toeplitz algebra $\mathcal T$ has a represnetation as a short exact sequence \[ 0\,\,\longrightarrow\,\,\mathcal T/\mathcal K\,\,\longrightarrow \mathcal T\,\,\longrightarrow\,\,C(\mathbb T)\,\,\longrightarrow\,\, 0, \] where $\mathcal K$ is a copy of the $C^*$-algebra of all compact operators on $\mathcal{H}_{DA}$. Hence, \[ \mathcal T/\mathcal K\,\,\simeq\,\, C(\mathbb T). \]
nodes.section: 8 The $C^*$-algebra associated to expandable discrete analytic functions
nodes.statement_short: Recall the Toeplitz extension, so $\mathcal T/\mathcal K\simeq C(\mathbb T)$.

nodes.name: Pass to quotient
nodes.statement: Since the left hand-side of \eqref{810} leaves $\mathcal K$ invariant, it follows that \[ \alpha_t\,\,:\,\,\mathcal T\,\,\longrightarrow\,\,\mathcal T \] passes to the quotient $\mathcal T/\mathcal K\,\,\simeq\,\, C(\mathbb T)$.
nodes.section: 8 The $C^*$-algebra associated to expandable discrete analytic functions
nodes.statement_short: $\alpha_t$ preserves $\mathcal K$, so passes to the quotient.

nodes.name: Multiplier implies Schur
nodes.statement: Assume first that $s\in\mathcal{O}$ is a contractive ${\lozenge}$-multiplier on $\mathbf{H}$. Then $s=s\lozenge1\in\mathbf{H}$ and hence $s=Ts_0$ for some $s_0\in\mathbf{H}_2$. Furthermore, let $f\in\mathbf{H}_2$. Since $s\lozenge(Tf)=T(s_0f)\in\mathbf{H}$, $s_0f\in\mathbf{H}_2.$ Since $$\|f\|_{\mathbf{H}_2}=\|Tf\|_\mathbf{H}\geq\|s\lozenge(Tf)\|_\mathbf{H}=\|T(s_0f)\|_\mathbf{H}=\|s_0f\|_{\mathbf{H}_2},$$ $s_0\in\mathscr{S}.$
nodes.section: 9 A reproducing kernel Hilbert space of entire functions
nodes.statement_short: A contractive multiplier is $Ts_0$ with $s_0$ Schur.

nodes.name: Schur implies multiplier
nodes.statement: Conversely, if $s=Ts_0$ where $s_0\in\mathscr{S}$, and $f\in\mathbf{H}_2$ then $s\lozenge(Tf)=T(s_0f)\in\mathbf{H}$ and $$\|s\lozenge(Tf)\|_\mathbf{H}=\|T(s_0f)\|_\mathbf{H}=\|s_0f\|_{\mathbf{H}_2} \leq\|f\|_{\mathbf{H}_2}=\|Tf\|_\mathbf{H}.$$ Thus $s$ is a contractive ${\lozenge}$-multiplier on $\mathbf{H}$.
nodes.section: 9 A reproducing kernel Hilbert space of entire functions
nodes.statement_short: Conversely $Ts_0$ is a contractive multiplier.

nodes.name: Reduction
nodes.statement: The claims follow from the definition of the operator $T$ in \eqref{opeT}. We prove only \eqref{r0}.
nodes.section: 9 A reproducing kernel Hilbert space of entire functions
nodes.statement_short: Only $\partial T=TR_0$ is proved.

nodes.name: Power series of f
nodes.statement: Let $f\in\mathbf H_2$ with power series expansion \[ f(z)=\sum_{n=0}^\infty a_nz^n. \]
nodes.section: 9 A reproducing kernel Hilbert space of entire functions
nodes.statement_short: Write $f$ as a power series.

nodes.name: Compute T R_0 f
nodes.statement: Then, \[ (R_0f)(z)=\sum_{n=1}^\infty a_nz^{n-1}, \] and therefore \[ \begin{split} (TR_0f)(z)&=\sum_{n=1}^\infty \frac{a_n}{(n-1)!}z^{n-1}\\ &=\frac{d}{dz}\left(\sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{a_n}{n!}z^n\right)\\ &=(\partial Tf)(z). \end{split} \]
nodes.section: 9 A reproducing kernel Hilbert space of entire functions
nodes.statement_short: Compute $TR_0f=\partial Tf$ termwise.

nodes.name: Pull back and translate invariance
nodes.statement: Let $H$ be a closed subspace of $\mathbf{H}$ then $H=TH_0$ where $H_0$ is a closed subspace of $\mathbf{H}_2$. $H$ is $\partial$-invariant if and only if $H_0$ is $R_0$-invariant, which is equivalent to $\mathbf{H}_2\ominus H_0$ being invariant under multiplication by $z$.
nodes.section: 9 A reproducing kernel Hilbert space of entire functions
nodes.statement_short: Write $H=TH_0$; $\partial$-invariance of $H$ is $R_0$-invariance of $H_0$.

nodes.name: Apply Beurling-Lax
nodes.statement: By the Beurling-Lax theorem, the last condition holds if and only if $\mathbf{H}_2\ominus H_0=M_{s_0}\mathbf{H}_2,$ where $s_0$ is an inner function.
nodes.section: 9 A reproducing kernel Hilbert space of entire functions
nodes.statement_short: Apply the Beurling-Lax theorem.

nodes.name: Realize s_0
nodes.statement: Write $s=Ts_0$, where $s_0\in\mathscr{S}$. Then $$s_0(z)=D_0+zC_0(I-zR_0)^{-1}B_0,$$ where $$\begin{pmatrix} R_0 & B_0\\ C_0& D_0\end{pmatrix}:\begin{pmatrix} H(s_0)\\ \mathbb{C}\end{pmatrix}\longrightarrow \begin{pmatrix} H(s_0)\\ \mathbb{C}\end{pmatrix}$$ is a coisometry given by \[ \nonumber \begin{split} R_0 f&=(f-f(0))/z,\\ B_01&=R_0s_0,\\ C_0f&=f(0),\\ D_01&=s_0(0)=s(0). \end{split} \]
nodes.section: 9 A reproducing kernel Hilbert space of entire functions
nodes.statement_short: Write $s=Ts_0$ and take the backward-shift realization of $s_0$.

nodes.name: Conjugate by T
nodes.statement: Hence \[ \nonumber \begin{split} s(z)&=D_0+\sum_{n=0}^\infty \dfrac{z^{n+1}}{(n+1)!} C_0R_0^nB_0\\ &=D_0+\sum_{n=0}^\infty \dfrac{z^{n+1}}{(n+1)!}C_0T^{-1}(TR_0T^{-1})^nTB_0\\ &=D+\sum_{n=0}^\infty \dfrac{z^{n+1}}{(n+1)!}C\partial^nB\\ &= D+\int_0^zCe^{t\partial}Bdt. \end{split} \]
nodes.section: 9 A reproducing kernel Hilbert space of entire functions
nodes.statement_short: Conjugate the realization by $T$ to get the integral formula.

nodes.name: Easy direction
nodes.statement: One direction follows immediately from Theorem \ref{s2}.
nodes.section: 9 A reproducing kernel Hilbert space of entire functions
nodes.statement_short: One direction from Theorem 9.4.

nodes.name: Point evaluation via exponential
nodes.statement: The proof of the other direction is modelled after the proof of \cite[Theorem 3.1.2, p. 85]{adrs} and is done as follows: let $H$ be $\partial$-invariant; then for every $f\in H$ $$Ce^{z\partial}f=f(z),$$ where $Cf=f(0).$
nodes.section: 9 A reproducing kernel Hilbert space of entire functions
nodes.statement_short: Following Alpay-Dijksma-Rovnyak-de Snoo, write $f(z)=Ce^{z\partial}f$.

nodes.name: Kernel formula
nodes.statement: Hence the reproducing kernel of $H$ is given by $$L_(z,w)=Ce^{z\partial}e^{w^*\partial^*}C^*.$$
nodes.section: 9 A reproducing kernel Hilbert space of entire functions
nodes.statement_short: Express the kernel via $\partial$ and $C$.

nodes.name: Coisometric extension
nodes.statement: Since $$\partial^*\partial+C^*C\leq I,$$ there exists a coisometry $$\begin{pmatrix} \partial & B\\ C& D\end{pmatrix}:\begin{pmatrix} H\\ \mathbb{C}\end{pmatrix}\longrightarrow \begin{pmatrix} H\\ \mathbb{C}\end{pmatrix}.$$
nodes.section: 9 A reproducing kernel Hilbert space of entire functions
nodes.statement_short: Complete $(\partial, C)$ to a coisometry.

nodes.name: Compare kernels
nodes.statement: But the the function $$s(z)=D+\int_0^zCe^{t\partial}Bdt$$ is a contractive ${\lozenge}$-multiplier and the associated kernel $K_s(z,w)$ coincides with $L(z,w)$. Hence $H=H(s).$
nodes.section: 9 A reproducing kernel Hilbert space of entire functions
nodes.statement_short: The associated multiplier has the same kernel, so $H=H(s)$.
